title: Diagnose product, portfolio and acquisition quality before funding any owned-media retention work
hypothesis: If we check product quality, portfolio and acquisition quality before spending on email, SMS or loyalty, then the spend actually works because owned media only amplifies a healthy retention system, it cannot fix a broken one.

signal.check: Budget or roadmap time is being planned for email, SMS, loyalty or delight work with no completed check of product, portfolio and acquisition quality first.

risk.note: A diagnostic step; no live change yet.

prerequisites: Review text, support tickets, refund reasons
Cohort repeat rate and LTGP by channel
steps: Pull review text, support ticket themes, refund reasons and NPS if collected.
List cross-sell, upsell or replenishment paths for the top 3 SKUs.
Compare repeat rate and LTGP by acquisition channel, AOV band and discount code.
Run the post-purchase journey and support audits.
Only then review engaged share, flow coverage and cadence.
Name the constraint and the evidence for it.

test.method: Confirm the named constraint against the next cohort's data before funding the matching fix.

title: Audit product quality using real customer evidence, never founder opinion
hypothesis: If we pull review text, support ticket themes, refund reasons and NPS instead of relying on founder opinion, then product fixes target what customers actually experience, not what the founder assumes.

signal.check: A product decision or CX budget was set from founder opinion with no review, ticket or refund-reason data behind it.

risk.note: A research step only.

prerequisites: Support ticket log tagged by type
steps: Pull review text and rating trend for the top SKUs.
Tag support tickets by theme: product, fit, quality, other.
Pull refund reasons for the same SKUs.
Compare against founder or team assumptions and note any gap.

test.method: Check whether the top named issue from the data matches what the team assumed before looking.

title: Check that the product portfolio gives customers a reason to come back
hypothesis: If we map cross-sell, upsell and replenishment paths for the top 3 SKUs, then a weak repeat rate gets fixed with a product or bundle change instead of more messaging aimed at a gap that messaging cannot close.

signal.check: No cross-sell, upsell or replenishment path exists for one or more top-selling SKUs.

expected_effect.size: unknown, depends on the product gap found

risk.note: A diagnostic and planning step.

steps: List the top 3 SKUs by revenue.
For each, name the cross-sell, upsell or replenishment path a customer could take next.
If none exists, flag it as a product or collection gap, not a messaging gap.
Route any gap to product or offer planning instead of a new email flow.

test.method: Track repeat rate for buyers of a top SKU before and after a new path is added.
test.read_point: 90 days after the new path launches

title: Audit whether first-order acquisition source predicts weak repeat behavior
hypothesis: If we compare repeat rate and LTGP by acquisition channel, AOV band and discount code, then low-quality acquisition gets caught as a retention problem instead of being blamed on email or CX.

signal.check: Repeat rate looks weak and no one has checked whether it is concentrated in one acquisition channel, low-AOV cohort or heavy discount code.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a diagnostic finding not a lever itself

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

prerequisites: Order-level data with acquisition source and discount code
steps: Split cohorts by acquisition channel.
Split cohorts by first-order AOV band.
Split cohorts by discount code used.
Compare repeat rate and LTGP across the splits.
Name any channel, band or code with a clear repeat-rate penalty.

test.method: Re-run the split after any acquisition mix change to see if the penalty shrinks or grows.

title: Track whether well-handled problems predict a customer's return visit
hypothesis: If we track repeat rate for customers who had a problem handled well against those with no problem, then customer experience gets credit as a retention lever, not just a cost line.

signal.check: Support and shipping problem resolution is tracked for cost only, with no link back to whether the customer bought again.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states a well-handled problem predicts return, no size given

risk.note: A measurement build, no process change.

prerequisites: Support ticket log linked to orders
steps: Tag orders that had a support contact or delivery problem.
Split into well-resolved versus poorly-resolved using CSAT or a manual read.
Compare 90-day repeat rate between the two groups and against customers with no problem.
Report the gap alongside the standard CX dashboard.

test.method: Recompute the gap each quarter as recovery practices change.

title: Diagnose weak first-to-second purchase conversion as a foundations problem before blaming email copy
hypothesis: If we check product, portfolio and acquisition quality before touching email copy, then a weak first-to-second conversion rate gets the right fix instead of a copy rewrite that cannot move a structural problem.

signal.check: First-to-second order conversion is weak and the response so far has only been email or SMS copy changes.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a diagnosis not a direct lever

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: Check whether attribution dashboards or the Shopify returning-customer metric are being used as proof retention is fine.
Run the retention hierarchy check (product, portfolio, acquisition, CX) before any copy work.
Only after that, review email and SMS copy in the F2 branch of each flow.

test.method: Compare F2 rate for a cohort before and after fixing the named foundational gap versus a copy-only change.
test.read_point: At the next cohort's F2 window

title: Map the account into 3 functions: acquisition, first-to-second conversion, and top-20% revenue
hypothesis: If we track acquisition volume, first-to-second order conversion and top-20% customer revenue as 3 separate functions, then the team always knows which one is the actual constraint instead of guessing.

signal.check: There is no report that separates acquisition volume, F2 rate and top-20% share as distinct, named functions.

risk.note: A reporting build.

prerequisites: Cohort data with acquisition volume, F2 rate, top-20% share
steps: Report new customers acquired per period as F1.
Report first-to-second order conversion within 90 days as F2.
Report revenue and profit share from the top 20% of customers as F3.
Compare all 3 against history and goals together, not separately.

test.method: Name the weakest of the 3 functions and check the team agrees before acting.

title: Split every marketing flow's first branch by journey stage: new, returning, loyal or subscriber
hypothesis: If every flow's first split is new versus returning versus loyal or subscriber instead of by product, then each group gets the right tone, aggression and offer instead of one message for everyone.

signal.check: A flow (welcome, abandonment, post-purchase) sends the same content regardless of whether the customer is new, returning or loyal.

risk.note: Rebuilding flow logic; test before full rollout to avoid breaking existing automations.

prerequisites: ESP access to edit flow logic
Customer status data: new, returning, loyal, subscriber
steps: Open every live flow and check the first split condition.
Rebuild the first split as new, returning, or loyal/subscriber.
Make new-customer branches more aggressive on trust and price.
Make returning branches skip the introduction.
Make loyal or subscriber branches the least aggressive, ideally with no incentive.
Move any product or cart-value split to a secondary, tested branch.

test.method: Compare F2 rate and repeat rate before and after the rebuild for a matched cohort.

title: Remove any single linear flow or product-first split that hides the real retention constraint
hypothesis: If we remove a one-size-fits-all linear sequence or a product-first first split, then the constraint (F1, F2 or F3) becomes visible instead of hidden inside an undifferentiated flow.

signal.check: A flow sends every entrant through one identical sequence, or the first split is by product attribute rather than journey stage.

risk.note: Flow logic change; test on a small segment first.

steps: List every live flow and its first split condition.
Flag any linear-for-everyone flow or product-first split.
Rebuild the first split as journey stage per the flow-structure idea.
Keep a product-attribute split only as a secondary, tested branch.

test.method: Check whether the constraint (F1, F2, F3) becomes clearer to name after the rebuild.

title: Route fixes straight to the constrained function's branch across every flow
hypothesis: If we go straight to the F2 branch (or whichever function is weak) across every flow once the constraint is known, then the fix targets the real gap instead of a generic new win-back flow or discount campaign.

signal.check: The constraint has been named (for example F2) but the response is a new generic flow or a blanket discount campaign instead of a targeted fix in the constrained branch.

risk.note: Flow logic change.

prerequisites: Named constraint from the F1/F2/F3 mapping
steps: Confirm the named constraint from the cohort readout.
Open every flow and go straight to that function's branch.
List the specific gaps in that branch across all flows.
Fix those gaps before adding any new flow.

test.method: Track the constrained function's metric for 90 days after the targeted fix.

title: Use flows for behavior-based sends and campaigns for reach, not the other way around
hypothesis: If flows carry the 24/7 behavior-triggered journey and campaigns carry broad reach and moments, then the incremental, always-on work does not get starved by blast-focused thinking.

signal.check: Most retention effort goes into one-off campaign blasts with little investment in the always-on flow architecture.

expected_effect.size: unknown, business and month dependent, not a fixed ratio

risk.note: A resourcing decision, not a live change by itself.

steps: Review current flow coverage: welcome, abandonment, post-purchase, win-back.
Review current campaign cadence and content mix.
Shift build time toward flow gaps found in the F1/F2/F3 audit.
Track the flow-to-campaign revenue split as a business signal, not a target ratio.

test.method: Watch whether flow revenue share rises after closing flow gaps.

title: Give first-time, repeat and VIP buyers different post-purchase content tracks
hypothesis: If first-time buyers get education and brand story, repeat buyers get cross-sell into adjacent categories, and VIPs get early access and recognition, then each group sees content matched to where they actually are.

signal.check: First-time, repeat and VIP customers currently see an identical on-site and email experience after purchase.

expected_effect.size: one segmented, non-discount re-engagement case reported a 29-point retention lift in 30 days

risk.note: Content and flow branching change; test before full rollout.

prerequisites: Customer tier data: first-time, repeat, VIP
steps: Tag customers as first-time, repeat or VIP.
Build a first-time track: education, brand story, trust-building.
Build a repeat track: cross-sell into adjacent categories.
Build a VIP track: early access, exclusive experiences, recognition.
Apply the same split to on-site content where the platform allows.

test.method: Compare repeat rate and engagement across the 3 tracks after 90 days.

title: Define an engaged audience as the primary sendable base and target 50 percent or more of the list
hypothesis: If we define engaged as opened, clicked, added to cart, started checkout or ordered within a set lookback, and target at least half the list inside it, then owned-media sends reach people likely to act instead of a dead list.

signal.check: There is no defined engaged segment, or the engaged share of the list is below 50% with no tracked trend.

risk.note: Segment build only.

steps: Set lookbacks by the brand's purchase cycle, adapting from about 180 days for email, 220 for site actions, 280 for orders.
Build the engaged segment from opens, clicks, add-to-cart, checkout starts and orders.
Set this as the primary sendable base for campaigns.
Track engaged share monthly as the core owned-media KPI.

test.method: Track engaged_share monthly and confirm it is rising toward 50%.

title: Rebuild dormant subscriber reach gradually with random samples instead of one full-list blast
hypothesis: If we split the unengaged list into equal random samples and add one sample per send, then dormant reach gets rebuilt without a single risky blast that could tank deliverability.

signal.check: A large share of the list is unengaged and the only reactivation plan on the table is one full-list send.

expected_effect.size: one 9-figure retailer case reported a 40% year-on-year lift after a rebuilt full-list send

risk.note: A bad sample send can hurt deliverability; the fix is to halve the sample size, not stop the rebuild.

prerequisites: ESP send capability with deliverability monitoring
steps: Split the unengaged remainder into about 10 equal random samples.
Each send, add 1 sample using the best-performing content.
Compute the newly engaged rate from that sample after the send.
Fold newly engaged subscribers into the permanent engaged segment.
Repeat over 6 to 9 months.
Save the biggest reactivation push for a calendar peak once the base is rebuilt.

test.method: Compute the actual newly_engaged_rate each round; if bounce or spam rate rises, halve the sample size.

title: Run 4 lifecycle cohorts for subscription brands by purchase and subscribe status
hypothesis: If we run 4 lifecycle cohorts each with 1 clear goal, then messaging matches exactly where a subscription customer sits instead of one generic flow for everyone.

signal.check: Subscription customers are messaged as one group with no lifecycle-stage segmentation.

risk.note: Segment and flow build.

steps: Tag customers as never purchased, purchased not subscribed, active subscriber, or cancelled.
For never purchased, aim for the first sale, ideally onto subscription.
For purchased not subscribed, aim to upsell to subscription or the next order.
For active subscriber, protect the relationship with no incentive.
For cancelled, aim to reactivate.

test.method: Track subscription churn and reactivation rate by cohort after launch.

does_not_apply_when: Non-subscription brands, which should use RFM or spend tiers instead

title: Score RFM segments against the brand's own base, not an external benchmark
hypothesis: If RFM segments (Champions, Loyal, Recent, At Risk, Needs Attention) are built from the brand's own order cadence, then the At Risk trigger fires at the right time for this brand's actual buying rhythm.

signal.check: RFM segmentation is missing, or is scored against a generic benchmark instead of the brand's own median reorder cadence.

risk.note: Segment build in the ESP.

steps: Compute the brand's own median days between orders.
Build RFM segments in the ESP's analytics tab relative to that cadence.
Export Champions, Loyal, Recent, At Risk and Needs Attention segments.
Treat Needs Attention like At Risk, especially for former Champions.

test.method: Check whether the At Risk trigger fires close to the brand's real median reorder point after 90 days.

title: Trigger win-back, replenishment and abandonment flows off RFM instead of a fixed day count
hypothesis: If flows trigger off a customer's own RFM cadence instead of a fixed day count, then a 200-day-cycle customer stops getting an unneeded discount 120 days in.

signal.check: Win-back, replenishment or abandonment flows use one fixed day count for every customer regardless of category or personal cadence.

risk.note: Flow trigger logic change.

steps: List every flow currently using a fixed day-count trigger.
Replace the trigger condition with the matching RFM segment (At Risk for win-back, for example).
Test the new trigger on a segment before full rollout.
Monitor unnecessary discount sends dropping.

test.method: Compare discount waste (discounts sent to customers who would have reordered anyway) before and after.

title: Define VIPs by revenue and profit concentration, validated on the brand's own data
hypothesis: If VIPs are defined by their actual share of revenue and profit instead of an assumed spend threshold, then the VIP program targets customers who really carry the business.

signal.check: There is no data-validated VIP definition, or VIP status is assigned by a guessed spend threshold.

expected_effect.size: one source's pattern: about 50% or more of revenue, about 80% of profit from the top 20%

risk.note: A definition step.

prerequisites: 12 months of order-level revenue and profit data
steps: Compute top-20%-by-revenue customer share of total revenue and profit for the trailing 12 months.
Compare against the roughly 50% revenue, 80% profit reference pattern.
Record the brand's own numbers as the VIP definition, not the reference pattern.
Revalidate the definition yearly.

test.method: Re-check the top-20% share against the VIP definition each year.

title: Invest in VIP-specific programming only when VIP revenue is the actual constraint
hypothesis: If VIP program work is funded only once VIP revenue is confirmed as the constraint and the brand is past small scale, then effort is not spent on VIPs while first-to-second order conversion is still the real problem.

signal.check: A VIP or loyalty program is planned or in progress while first-to-second order conversion is still weak and the brand is under roughly 10 to 20 million a year.

risk.note: A go/no-go decision on a planned program.

steps: Check whether F2 (first-to-second conversion) is the named constraint from the cohort readout.
If F2 is weak and revenue is under roughly 10 to 20 million a year, pause VIP program work.
Route the freed effort to the F2 fix instead.
Revisit VIP investment once F2 and scale both clear the bar.

test.method: Re-check the named constraint each quarter to see when VIP investment becomes justified.

does_not_apply_when: Brands above roughly 10 to 20 million a year where VIP revenue already has leverage

title: Report customer value as lifetime gross profit, never as revenue
hypothesis: If we report LTV as lifetime gross profit instead of revenue, then spend and CAC decisions get safer because unit economics differ store to store and revenue alone hides that.

signal.check: The retention dashboard or any deck still says LTV or lifetime value in revenue terms with no cost line subtracted.

risk.note: Only a reporting change; no live system is touched.

steps: List every place LTV or lifetime value appears in reports and decks.
Replace each with lifetime gross profit, built from revenue minus COGS, delivery, fees and refunds.
Re-label the dashboard column and any saved report.
Tell the team the new number is not comparable to the old one.

test.method: Compare a CAC decision made on revenue LTV against the same decision made on LTGP for one cohort.

title: Attach a time window to every LTV or LTGP figure reported
hypothesis: If we always state the window with every LTGP number (30 day, 90 day, 365 day), then decisions stop mixing incomparable numbers because a bare lifetime figure cannot be measured or compared.

signal.check: A report, deck or dashboard shows LTV or LTGP with no day count next to it.

risk.note: Labeling change only.

steps: Build the cohort LTGP curve at 0, 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days.
Add the window to every LTGP label, for example 90-day LTGP.
Reject any chart or slide that drops the window.
Refresh the curve at least monthly.

test.method: Audit 5 recent reports for a bare LTV number with no window.

title: Build LTGP from order-level revenue and refund lines, not an assumed margin
hypothesis: If we compute LTGP from real order, COGS, delivery, fee and refund lines instead of AOV times an assumed margin, then the number stays accurate through discount periods because AOV and margin move together and a flat assumption breaks then.

signal.check: LTGP or cohort profit is currently computed as average order value times one fixed margin percentage.

expected_effect.size: unknown, accuracy gain not a size

risk.note: Read-only calculation change; no customer-facing effect.

prerequisites: Order-level export with customer id, order date, revenue, refund lines
steps: Assign each customer to the cohort of their first order.
For each order, subtract COGS, delivery, fees and refund allowance from revenue.
Sum per cohort and divide by cohort size for each window.
Refresh the build at least monthly and flag discount-period cohorts.

test.method: Compare the AOV-times-margin estimate against the order-level build for one discount-period cohort.
test.read_point: After the next discount period closes

title: Count refunds in LTGP only, never in the CAC denominator
hypothesis: If we subtract refunds from LTGP only and keep the CAC denominator as the pre-refund new-customer count, then CAC stops being blamed for a product problem it did not cause.

signal.check: Refunded customers are being removed from the new-customer count used in CAC, or refunds are subtracted from both CAC and LTGP.

risk.note: Calculation fix only.

prerequisites: Confirmation of whether revenue feed is gross or net of refunds
steps: Check whether the revenue feed already nets out refunds.
If gross, subtract a refund allowance inside LTGP only.
If net, set the refund allowance to 0 so refunds are not double counted.
Keep the CAC new-customer count as the pre-refund count, always.

test.method: Recompute CAC and LTGP for one period both ways and compare.

title: Set the CAC reporting period by store scale
hypothesis: If we report CAC daily or hourly for large retailers and weekly or monthly for smaller brands, then the number matches how fast the business can actually react instead of being noise at one scale or lagging at the other.

signal.check: CAC is reported at a fixed period regardless of order volume, and it is either too noisy to act on or too slow to catch a spend problem.

risk.note: Reporting cadence change only.

steps: Estimate current annual revenue scale.
Pick daily or hourly reporting for 9 to 10 figure retailers.
Pick weekly or monthly reporting for 6 to 8 figure brands.
Rebuild the CAC report at the new period and compare noise against the old one.

test.method: Compare week to week CAC variance at the old and new reporting period.
test.read_point: After 4 weeks at the new period

title: Set a CAC target from LTGP using a 2 to 3 target ratio
hypothesis: If we set the CAC target as LTGP at a stated window divided by a ratio inside the 2 to 3 band, then spend gets managed against a real ceiling instead of habit or a competitor's number.

signal.check: There is no written CAC target, or the target does not trace back to an LTGP number and a stated ratio.

risk.note: Setting a target does not itself change spend; it is a planning input.

prerequisites: 90-day or chosen-window LTGP from the cohort build
steps: Pick the LTGP window per the window-choice idea.
Pick a target ratio inside 2.0 to 3.0 unless a funded growth plan states otherwise.
Compute CAC target as LTGP at that window divided by the ratio.
Write down the formula used: LTGP_W divided by ratio equals target.
Re-run the target at least quarterly.

test.method: Compare actual CAC against the written target each period.

title: Choose the LTGP measurement window by capital position and category, not habit
hypothesis: If we default to a 30-day LTGP window for bootstrapped or sub-scale brands and 90-day or further for high-repeat or funded brands, then the CAC ceiling matches what the business can actually afford to wait for.

signal.check: The LTGP window used for CAC decisions was picked once and never revisited against current capital and category.

expected_effect.size: moving from 30-day to 90-day raised the ceiling 25% in one worked example

risk.note: Choosing a window is a planning decision with no direct customer effect.

steps: Confirm annual revenue and capital position (bootstrapped, funded, loan).
Confirm category repeat cycle: consumable, durable, fashion.
Default to 30-day for bootstrapped or under about 15 to 20 million a year.
Use 90-day or further for CPG, supplements or funded brands willing to run a short-term loss.
Write down the reason for the chosen window.

test.method: Recompute the CAC target and ceiling under both the 30-day and 90-day window and compare.

does_not_apply_when: A loan-funded model under about 15 to 20 million a year without interest-cost modeling

title: Forecast incremental customer volume before raising the CAC ceiling
hypothesis: If we plot new customers against the CAC ceiling before raising it, then the business only funds a higher ceiling when it buys meaningfully more customers, not on hope.

signal.check: The CAC ceiling is about to be raised with no forecast of how many extra customers that buys.

expected_effect.size: one worked example showed 30% to 40% more customers per 10 unit ceiling rise

risk.note: A wrong forecast leads to overspending, but the decision is reversible by lowering the ceiling again.

prerequisites: CAC target from the window-and-ratio idea
Historical new-customer volume at different CAC levels
steps: Plot new customers acquired against CAC ceiling using recent history.
Estimate incremental customers per unit rise in the ceiling.
Fund the higher ceiling only if the volume gain is meaningful and cash allows.
Stay conservative if the volume barely moves.

test.method: Track actual new customers acquired for 4 weeks after raising the ceiling against the forecast.

title: Bound CAC with a floor and a realistic case built from CPC and new-customer conversion
hypothesis: If we compute a CAC floor from the best CPC and conversion rate and a realistic case from current numbers, then the business knows how much headroom paid spend actually has left before chasing it further.

signal.check: There is no computed CAC floor, or CAC is judged from cost per click alone.

risk.note: A calculation, not a spend change.

prerequisites: CPC data, best case and current
New-customer conversion rate, not all-purchase conversion
steps: Compute new-customer conversion as new customers divided by clicks, not all purchases.
Compute the floor as best CPC divided by best new-customer conversion.
Compute the realistic case as current CPC divided by current conversion.
Report paid headroom as realistic minus floor.

test.method: Recompute paid headroom monthly and watch the trend.

title: Decide whether CAC or LTGP has more room before investing effort
hypothesis: If we check paid headroom before deciding where to invest, then effort goes to the side with real room instead of chasing a CAC floor that traffic quality has already reached.

signal.check: Paid headroom is small (realistic CAC is close to the floor) but the team keeps trying to lower CAC further instead of raising LTGP.

risk.note: A prioritization decision with no direct execution risk.

prerequisites: Paid headroom from the CAC floor idea
steps: Compute paid headroom (realistic CAC minus floor).
If headroom is small, route effort to LTGP levers: offers, subscription, retention.
If headroom is large, route effort to paid efficiency work instead.
Re-check quarterly since the answer can flip.

test.method: Compare where effort was actually spent against where the headroom pointed, one quarter later.

title: Track the CAC payback day for subscription or CPG brands taking a Day-0 loss
hypothesis: If we track the day cumulative cohort gross profit crosses total CAC, then the business can see and plan around the working capital tied up in scaling, instead of guessing.

signal.check: The brand takes a loss on the first order and there is no tracked payback day on the finance dashboard.

risk.note: Tracking only; the deficit already exists regardless of measurement.

steps: Confirm the category has real replenishment or subscription depth.
Compute the Day-0 deficit as CAC minus Day-0 gross profit.
Track cumulative cohort gross profit through time.
Mark the day cumulative profit first meets or exceeds CAC.
Model the working capital tied up before that day, per month of spend.

test.method: Track the payback day for 3 consecutive cohorts and check if it is getting earlier or later.

does_not_apply_when: One-off or durable-goods purchase categories with no repeat cycle

title: Test offer and subscription changes to raise the LTGP ceiling
hypothesis: If we test bundles, starter kits, multi-month packs and subscribe-and-save against the current 90 and 365 day LTGP ceiling, then the ceiling moves because the offer changes how much a customer buys over time, not just on the first order.

signal.check: The LTGP ceiling has not moved in a review cycle and no offer or subscription test is running against it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, varies by offer and category

risk.note: A failed offer test can lower short-term AOV; keep it reversible and time-boxed.

prerequisites: Current subscription attach rate if any
steps: Map the current 90 and 365 day LTGP ceiling including subscription attach.
Pick one offer variant to test: bundle, starter kit, multi-month pack, or trial vs full size.
Judge the result by cohort LTGP, never first-order AOV alone.
Treat any rise in subscription cancellation as a leading negative signal.
Re-run the LTGP:CAC ratio after the change.

test.method: Compare cohort LTGP for the test offer against a matched control cohort.
test.read_point: At the LTGP window used for the ratio, plus 2 weeks for refunds

title: Value customers and visitors by margin, not revenue or order count
hypothesis: If we rank customers and visitors by gross margin contribution instead of revenue or order count, then spend and attention go to the buyers who actually make the business money.

signal.check: Customer or visitor value ranking is based on revenue or order count with no per-SKU cost data behind it.

expected_effect.size: one vendor case reported a 72% margin boost

risk.note: Requires clean per-SKU COGS; a dirty COGS feed makes this directional only.

steps: Confirm per-SKU COGS quality before using margin as a ranking metric.
Compute basket margin per customer or visitor.
Re-rank customer and channel value by margin instead of revenue.
Track the margin trajectory over time, not a single snapshot.

test.method: Compare a spend or attention decision made on revenue ranking against the same decision on margin ranking.

does_not_apply_when: Per-SKU COGS data is not clean or complete

title: Stop using Shopify's percent-returning-customers metric as a retention KPI
hypothesis: If we replace Shopify's percent-returning-customers metric with cohort repeat rate, then the business stops rewarding weaker acquisition, since the old metric rises simply when fewer new customers are acquired.

signal.check: A dashboard or report cites percent returning customers as a retention or LTV signal.

risk.note: A reporting change only.

prerequisites: Order-level data with customer id and first-order date
steps: Find every report or dashboard using percent returning customers as a KPI.
Replace it with cohort repeat_rate_W (customers in a cohort with 2 or more orders within W days).
Keep the old metric only to slice a sale period into new versus existing resonance.

test.method: Compare the two metrics' trend lines over the last 6 months to confirm they tell different stories.

title: Report every retention metric by acquisition cohort, never as a blended average
hypothesis: If we report WISMO rate, repeat rate, NPS or LTGP by acquisition cohort instead of as one blended number, then acquisition timing and category mix stop hiding real changes in the metric.

signal.check: A retention or CX metric is reported as one company-wide average with no cohort or period breakdown.

risk.note: A reporting format change.

steps: Identify every retention metric currently reported as one blended number.
Rebuild each as a per-cohort series.
Present the cohort trend, not a single point, in every readout.

test.method: Check whether a metric that looked flat blended shows a real trend once split by cohort.

title: Treat platform attribution as directional only, and use profit metrics to find the real constraint
hypothesis: If we stop chasing in-platform attributed revenue and use cohort profit metrics to find the constraint instead, then decisions stop optimizing for looking good inside one tool.

signal.check: Campaign or flow decisions are being made mainly to move an in-platform attributed revenue number.

risk.note: A decision-process change, no live system change.

prerequisites: Cohort LTGP and repeat rate data
steps: List the decisions currently driven mainly by platform-attributed revenue.
For each, add cohort LTGP, repeat rate or top-20% share as the real deciding metric.
Keep attribution as a directional north star, not the target.

test.method: Track whether a decision changes once profit metrics are added alongside attribution.

title: Build one core retention dashboard around LTGP, first-to-second conversion and top-20% share
hypothesis: If we build one dashboard with 90 and 365 day LTGP, first-to-second conversion and top-20% revenue share as the headline numbers, then the team reads the same 3 numbers instead of scattered attribution submetrics.

signal.check: There is no single retention dashboard, or the current one leads with attribution or vanity metrics instead of LTGP, F2 rate and top-20% share.

risk.note: A reporting build; does not touch live systems.

steps: Build 90 and 365 day LTGP mapped across cohorts, refunds included.
Add first-to-second order conversion (F10) per cohort.
Add revenue and profit share from the top 20% of customers (F11).
Put campaign revenue, pop-up conversion and flow revenue underneath as submetrics.
Share the dashboard with the team as the single source of truth.

test.method: Ask the team which dashboard they check first, before and after the build.

title: Track delight-related retention metrics beyond CSAT and NPS
hypothesis: If we track CLV by delight-touchpoint cohort, WISMO volume, unboxing UGC count, return-to-repurchase rate, tracking-page engagement and loyalty-redeemer repeat rate, then a customer quietly drifting away shows up before CSAT or NPS would ever catch it.

signal.check: Only CSAT or NPS sit on the CX dashboard, with none of the behavioral retention metrics tracked.

risk.note: A reporting build.

steps: List the 6 metrics: delight-cohort CLV, WISMO volume, unboxing UGC count, return-to-repurchase rate, tracking-page engagement, loyalty-redeemer repeat rate.
Build a monthly view for each.
Add customer retention rate (F15) alongside if the population is stable enough to define.
Review all of them together with CSAT and NPS, not instead of them.

test.method: Check whether any of the 6 metrics moves before CSAT or NPS does over one quarter.

title: Judge a pop-up or sign-up form by the value of the customers it signs up, not its opt-in rate
hypothesis: If we measure a pop-up by the conversion, AOV and gross profit of the people it signs up instead of its opt-in percentage, then the metric stops rewarding a form that captures cheap, low-value emails.

signal.check: The pop-up or sign-up form is judged only by opt-in rate against a target percentage with no reference to signup quality.

risk.note: A measurement change; the pop-up itself is untouched.

prerequisites: Order data joined to sign-up source
steps: Tag customers by their sign-up source, including the pop-up.
Compute conversion rate, AOV and gross profit for pop-up-sourced customers.
Compare against other acquisition sources, not against an arbitrary opt-in target.
Reject an opt-in target set only because it is a common number.

test.method: Compare pop-up-sourced customer value against the next-best acquisition source after one full cohort matures.

title: Reward VIP customers with exclusivity, not broad discounts
hypothesis: If VIPs get exclusive products, private sales, early access and recognition instead of broad discounts, then the top tier stays loyal without training them to wait for markdowns.

signal.check: VIP or top-spend customers are receiving the same discount codes as the general list.

risk.note: A messaging and offer change to an existing segment.

steps: Build a dedicated VIP branch in relevant flows.
Replace any discount code sent to VIPs with exclusive products, early access, events or recognition.
Use the specific-goal campaign slot for VIP sends instead of the broad list.
Track VIP repeat rate and discount reliance before and after.

test.method: Compare VIP discount reliance and repeat rate 90 days before and after the change.

title: Spend about 80 percent of campaign effort on broad reach content and 20 percent on specific-goal sends
hypothesis: If most campaign effort goes to broad, engaging content for the whole engaged base and only a small share to narrow specific-goal sends, then a large audience is built that cashes in at peaks instead of a fragmented list that never builds momentum.

signal.check: Most campaigns target narrow micro-segments with a specific offer, and little content is aimed at the whole engaged base.

risk.note: A content-mix and calendar change.

steps: Audit the last quarter's campaigns for reach versus specific-goal content.
Set a rough 80/20 split toward broad reach content going forward.
Reserve specific-goal sends for a stated business reason: excess stock, a supplier sale, a product push, a VIP push.
Track engaged share growth over the next quarter.

test.method: Track engaged share trend over one quarter after rebalancing the calendar.

title: Reject hyperpersonalized micro-segmentation as the default campaign strategy
hypothesis: If campaigns stop being split into many one-to-one micro-segments by default, then the team can learn what broad content actually works instead of fragmenting effort across segments too small to read.

signal.check: Campaigns are routinely split into many small, one-to-one style segments with no clear payback on the added labor.

risk.note: A process change; reduces campaign complexity.

steps: Review the last quarter's campaign segment count and the labor spent building them.
Consolidate campaigns back to broad reach content for the engaged base as the default.
Reserve real personalization for flows, on-site and quiz-driven fit instead.
Track whether learning speed on 'what content works' improves.

test.method: Compare campaign build time and content-learning speed before and after consolidation.

title: Route real personalization into flows and on-site experience, not into campaign sends
hypothesis: If personalization work goes into flows and on-site recommendations instead of campaign blasts, then it acts on real behavior instead of guessing who in a static list is ready to buy today.

signal.check: Personalization effort (dynamic content, segment logic) is being built mainly into one-off campaigns rather than behavior-triggered flows or on-site.

risk.note: A resourcing shift.

steps: List current personalization work and where it lives: flows, campaigns, or on-site.
Shift new personalization build toward flows first, since they act on real behavior.
Split flows by journey stage first, then by product or collection as a secondary test.
Keep campaigns broad, aimed at the roughly 97% of the list not ready to buy today.

test.method: Compare conversion rate from flow-based personalization against the prior campaign-based approach.

title: Plan the marketing calendar in 2 layers: always-on baseline content and event-based peak campaigns
hypothesis: If the calendar separates always-on engagement content from event-based peak campaigns, then the channel gets judged by year-on-year growth relative to the business instead of by any single send.

signal.check: The campaign calendar has no clear split between baseline always-on content and event-based peaks like sales, launches or restocks.

risk.note: A calendar planning change.

steps: Map the last year of campaigns into baseline versus peak events.
Build a recurring always-on content layer for baseline weeks.
Reserve event-based peaks for sales, launches and restocks.
Judge the channel by year-on-year growth relative to the business, not by a single send's result.

test.method: Compare year-on-year owned-media growth against total business growth after one full cycle.

title: Default to little or no paid ad spend on existing customers
hypothesis: If paid spend on existing customers stays at little or none by default, then acquisition budget is not diluted chasing customers owned media can already reach for free.

signal.check: Meaningful paid budget is going toward retargeting or reaching existing customers with no stated exception reason.

risk.note: A budget reallocation; Meta stays read-only, this is a recommendation only.

prerequisites: Current ad spend breakdown by new versus existing customer
steps: Pull the current spend split between new and existing customer targeting.
Confirm whether the brand is fashion or frequent-drop, the only stated exception.
If not, recommend reallocating existing-customer spend to acquisition.
If it is the exception, apply the CPA and budget rules from the paired ideas.

test.method: Track new-customer volume and CAC after reallocating existing-customer spend.

does_not_apply_when: Fashion or frequent-drop brands where email and SMS cannot reach the whole base for new arrivals

title: Set the existing-customer ad CPA target at half or less of the new-customer CPA target
hypothesis: If the existing-customer CPA target is set at half or less of the new-customer target, then equal CPAs stop signaling overspend on customers who should convert more cheaply.

signal.check: Existing-customer ad spend is running (fashion or frequent-drop exception) with no CPA target set below the new-customer target.

expected_effect.size: example: 40 new-customer CPA implies 20 or lower existing-customer target

risk.note: A target-setting step; Meta remains read-only.

steps: Confirm the exception case applies (R49).
Set the existing-customer CPA target at half or less of the new-customer target.
Report actual existing-customer CPA against this target weekly.
Flag and investigate any period where existing CPA equals or exceeds new CPA.

test.method: Track existing-customer CPA against the target for 4 weeks.

title: Measure the marginal CAC of an existing-customer ad spend increase and pull back when it exceeds target
hypothesis: If the marginal cost of each extra existing-customer conversion is measured between 2 spend levels, then spend gets pulled back before it quietly drifts past the CPA target.

signal.check: Existing-customer ad spend has been raised with no marginal CAC check between the old and new spend level.

expected_effect.size: example: raising spend from 700 to 1000 a day bought 3 extra conversions at 100 each

risk.note: A measurement and reallocation step; Meta stays read-only.

prerequisites: 2 spend levels with conversion data for the same campaign
steps: Record conversions at a lower and a higher spend level.
Compute marginal CAC as the spend difference divided by the conversion difference.
Compare marginal CAC against the existing-customer CPA target.
Recommend pulling spend back to the lower level and reallocating the saving to acquisition if marginal CAC exceeds target.

test.method: Re-run the marginal CAC check every 2 weeks while existing-customer spend is active.

title: Budget existing-customer ad spend as a dollar figure from frequency and audience size, not a spend share
hypothesis: If the existing-customer budget is computed from send frequency, audience size and CPM instead of as a percentage of total spend, then the number matches what the audience actually needs to be reached, not an arbitrary share.

signal.check: Existing-customer spend is set as a percentage of the total ad budget rather than computed from audience size and reach frequency.

risk.note: A budgeting formula change; Meta remains read-only.

steps: Confirm the fashion or frequent-drop exception applies.
Set send frequency between 4 and 7 times a month.
Compute the budget as frequency times existing customers times CPM divided by 1000.
Present this dollar figure as a recommendation, not an automatic ad-account change.

test.method: Compare the computed budget against the current percentage-of-spend budget.

title: Run a discount-cohort audit before scaling any promotion
hypothesis: If repeat rate and LTGP are compared between discount-code and no-code cohorts before scaling a promotion, then a promotion that quietly damages long-term value gets caught before it is scaled.

signal.check: A discount or promo code is being considered for scaling with no comparison of repeat rate or LTGP against the no-code cohort.

expected_effect.size: one source reports about 60% of client brands see substantially worse LTV from discount-acquired cohorts

risk.note: A diagnostic step before a spend decision.

prerequisites: Order-level data with discount code per order
steps: Split cohorts by discount code used on the first order, including a no-code group.
Compute repeat_rate_90, repeat_rate_365, ltgp_90 and ltgp_365 per group.
Compute the penalty per code against the no-code group.
Weigh the front-end lift (ROAS, volume) against the penalty before scaling.
State both sides in numbers in the recommendation.

test.method: Re-run the audit after the promotion scales to confirm the penalty held or changed.

title: Run a zero-party persona audit on the top and bottom 20 percent of customers
hypothesis: If the top and bottom 20% of customers are analyzed for shared persona, angle and offer, then paid spend can overallocate toward the winning pattern and cut the angles that attract mismatched buyers.

signal.check: There is no analysis comparing the persona, acquisition angle and first offer of the highest-value and lowest-value customers.

risk.note: A research step feeding a creative and targeting recommendation.

prerequisites: Post-purchase survey or quiz data joined to orders
12-month revenue or gross profit per customer
steps: Rank customers by 12-month revenue or gross profit.
Take the top and bottom 20%.
Tabulate persona, acquisition angle, first offer, refund and repeat rate for each group.
Name the top-20% pattern to overallocate spend toward.
Name bottom-20% mismatches to reduce or exclude, even where front-end ROAS looks strong.
Hand the angle changes to the creative and deployment teams.

test.method: Track refund and repeat rate for the adjusted angle mix after one full cohort matures.

title: Check refunds and repeat rate before trusting a strong front-end ROAS on any ad angle
hypothesis: If refunds, returns and repeat rate are checked for any angle showing strong front-end ROAS, then a mismatched angle that only looks good on the ad dashboard gets caught before more budget goes to it.

signal.check: An ad angle or campaign shows unusually strong ROAS with no check of downstream refund or repeat behavior.

expected_effect.size: one cited case: a strong-ROAS angle led to high returns, refunds and no repeat

risk.note: A verification step before scaling spend.

prerequisites: Refund and repeat data joined to acquisition angle
steps: List any angle or campaign with unusually strong front-end ROAS.
Pull refund rate, return rate and repeat rate for customers from that angle.
Flag any angle with strong ROAS but weak downstream numbers.
Exclude or reduce spend on flagged angles even if the ad dashboard still looks strong.

test.method: Recheck downstream numbers for any newly scaled angle after 30 days.

title: Decide the intended feeling for each post-purchase touchpoint before writing its copy
hypothesis: If the intended feeling (reassured, informed, delighted) is decided before writing confirmation, tracking or return copy, then the copy is designed around that feeling instead of around urgency tactics that risk trust.

signal.check: Post-purchase copy (confirmation, tracking, returns) was written without first deciding what the customer should feel at that moment.

risk.note: A copywriting process step.

prerequisites: List of post-purchase touchpoints and their current copy
steps: List every post-purchase touchpoint: confirmation, tracking, wait, delivery, unboxing.
For each, name the 1 feeling the copy should produce.
Rewrite copy and timing around that feeling.
Remove urgency tactics like 'only 1 left' from post-purchase messages.

test.method: Read customer replies or support tickets tied to the touchpoint for tone shifts after the rewrite.

title: Fix effort and broken promises before adding any delight spend
hypothesis: If effort problems (late delivery, hard returns, slow refunds) are fixed before any delight spend, then delight spend actually builds loyalty instead of creating cognitive dissonance on top of a broken promise.

signal.check: A delight project (packaging, gifts, notes) is being planned or funded while a known effort problem, like late delivery or slow refunds, is still live.

expected_effect.size: one cited study found 96% of high-effort customers became more disloyal versus 9% of low-effort customers

risk.note: A sequencing decision, low execution risk.

prerequisites: Delivery estimate accuracy and refund cycle time data
steps: Check current delivery estimate accuracy, WISMO rate and refund cycle time.
Pause or delay any delight spend if a foundational effort problem is still open.
Fix the effort problem first.
Only then resume or launch the delight project.

test.method: Confirm the effort metric has cleared its threshold before the delight spend goes live.

title: Split the post-purchase journey into service moments and discretionary moments and treat them differently
hypothesis: If service moments get effort reduction and discretionary moments get engineered peaks, then delight spend goes where it works and effort gets cut where it matters most.

signal.check: The journey map, if one exists, does not classify touchpoints as service versus discretionary moments.

risk.note: A classification and planning step.

steps: List every touchpoint: checkout, returns, WISMO, complaints, unboxing, onboarding, milestones.
Classify each as a service moment (reduce effort) or a discretionary moment (build a peak).
For service moments, plan one-touch resolution, fast refunds, proactive updates, no dark patterns.
For discretionary moments, plan a limited number of peaks using elevation, insight, pride or connection.

test.method: Review the classification against customer feedback after 90 days to confirm the split still holds.

title: Fund 1 deliberate peak and 1 strong ending in the journey, not an even spread of spend
hypothesis: If spend concentrates on 1 clear peak (usually unboxing) and 1 strong ending (delivery confirmation or issue resolution), then memory of the experience improves because memory is set by the peak and the end, not the average.

signal.check: CX or delight spend is spread evenly across many touchpoints with no single funded peak or ending.

expected_effect.size: cited 2022 meta-analysis of 174 effect sizes supports peak-end memory effect

risk.note: A budget reallocation across the journey.

steps: Map the current journey and mark where spend and attention currently go.
Identify the natural peak candidate, usually physical unboxing.
Identify the natural ending candidate, usually delivery confirmation or issue resolution.
Concentrate discretionary spend on those 2 moments and cut even spread elsewhere.

test.method: Compare review sentiment and UGC volume for the funded peak and ending against the prior even-spread approach.

title: Find and fix the journey's negative peak before funding any new delight
hypothesis: If the worst moment in the journey (checkout friction, opaque billing, a slow refund) is found and fixed first, then it stops overriding a good average experience and wasting new delight spend.

signal.check: A delight project is planned while checkout friction, opaque billing, surprise fees or a slow refund process is still live somewhere in the journey.

risk.note: A diagnostic and fix-prioritization step.

prerequisites: Journey map or support ticket themes
steps: List candidate negative peaks: checkout friction, confusing navigation, opaque billing, surprise fees, broken delivery, slow refunds.
Confirm which one is currently live using support tickets or a live-order walkthrough.
Fix that negative peak before funding any new delight spend.
Re-check for a new negative peak after the fix.

test.method: Check whether the negative peak reappears in feedback 60 days after the fix.

title: Classify every touchpoint with the Kano model before budgeting any fix or delight spend
hypothesis: If every touchpoint is classified as must-be, one-dimensional or attractive before budgeting, then must-be gaps get funded as non-negotiable fixes and delight budget only goes to genuinely attractive items.

signal.check: There is no Kano classification behind the current CX or delight budget, so fixes and delight spend are not clearly separated.

risk.note: A classification step ahead of budgeting.

prerequisites: List of candidate touchpoints or fixes
steps: List every touchpoint under consideration for a fix or delight spend.
Classify each as must-be, one-dimensional or attractive.
Fund every must-be gap as a non-negotiable fix.
Hold one-dimensional items at market standard.
Send delight budget only to attractive items.
Re-run the classification periodically since it shifts across audiences and time.

test.method: Confirm no must-be gap remains open before any attractive-item spend is approved.

title: Plan for delight decay and put every funded delighter on a rotation cycle
hypothesis: If every funded delighter is expected to decay into a baseline expectation over time, then its replacement gets planned on a rolling cycle instead of the budget quietly becoming wasted spend.

signal.check: A funded delight item (free shipping, a gift, a note) has been running for a long time with no check on whether its impact has flattened.

risk.note: A monitoring and rotation process.

prerequisites: Metric history for each funded delighter
steps: List every currently funded delighter and its governing metric.
Track that metric's trend over time, not just its current value.
When the metric goes flat while spend continues, treat it as decayed.
Plan a replacement delighter on a rolling cycle rather than letting the old one run forever.

test.method: Check the metric trend for each delighter every quarter.

title: Never manufacture a failure to trigger a recovery moment; only over-recover real failures
hypothesis: If recovery moments are only used for real failures and never manufactured, then trust stays intact because error-free service still beats even a great recovery on customer satisfaction.

signal.check: A team idea proposes deliberately delaying, understocking or complicating an order to create a recovery moment.

expected_effect.size: one cited banking study found only 5.4% of problem customers rated recovery much better than expected; error-free service still won on satisfaction

risk.note: A policy decision, not a live change.

steps: State as policy that failures are never manufactured as a marketing tactic.
Reserve over-recovery actions (refund without escalation, human gesture, same-day replacement) for genuine failures only.
Brief support and fulfillment staff on this distinction.

test.method: Audit a sample of recovery cases quarterly to confirm none were manufactured.

title: Run a delight payback test before scaling any packaging, gift or note program
hypothesis: If a matched or randomized treated-versus-control test measures whether a delight program's incremental profit beats its per-customer cost, then packaging, gift or note spend gets scaled only once it actually pays back.

signal.check: A packaging, gift or handwritten-note program is running or planned with no test comparing its incremental profit against its cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states the test decides pass or fail, no universal size

risk.note: Running the test itself is low risk; the risk is in continuing an unproven program at scale.

prerequisites: CAC and first-order gross profit already computed
Ability to split matched or randomized cohorts
steps: Estimate the program's cost per customer (packaging, gift, note).
Split matched or randomized treated and control cohorts from the same acquisition period.
Observe over a mature window, at least the median second-order interval, ideally 90 days.
Compute incremental contribution: repeat gross profit gained minus remarketing, incentive and service cost.
Compare incremental contribution against the delight cost per customer.
If it fails, cut the per-order budget or change the program rather than change the accounting.

test.method: Compute incremental_contribution and compare it against delight_cost_per_customer.
test.read_point: At least 90 days, or the brand's median second-order interval

title: Turn the order confirmation into an anxiety-reduction message, not a receipt
hypothesis: If the confirmation includes a clear delivery estimate, the branded tracking link, what happens next, and 1 piece of value, then post-purchase anxiety drops instead of being left to a bare receipt.

signal.check: The order confirmation email reads as a plain receipt with no delivery estimate, tracking link, next-steps line or value-add content.

expected_effect.size: one source claims two-thirds of shoppers feel anxious right after buying

risk.note: A content edit to an existing transactional email.

prerequisites: Branded tracking page in place or in progress
steps: Add a clear delivery estimate to the confirmation.
Add the branded tracking link.
State what happens next in plain words.
Add 1 small piece of value: a care guide, styling tip or founder note.
Use concrete words like 'today' and 'update' instead of vague reassurance.

test.method: Track WISMO tickets per order for 30 days after the rewrite.

title: Send at least 3 proactive automated updates between order and delivery
hypothesis: If confirmation, shipping confirmation and out-for-delivery messages all send automatically, then WISMO tickets drop because customers get told before they have to ask.

signal.check: Fewer than 3 automated updates currently fire between order placement and delivery.

expected_effect.size: one source claims a 3-step flow can eliminate up to 80% of WISMO tickets

risk.note: A flow build in the existing ESP; test before full rollout.

steps: Count current automated touchpoints between order and delivery.
Build or confirm: order confirmation with delivery estimate, shipping confirmation with a working tracking link, out-for-delivery with a window.
Add delivered and delayed messages as a further step.
Check WISMO per order monthly after launch.

test.method: Track WISMO tickets per order shipped, monthly, for 3 months after launch.

title: Build the delivery estimate from real carrier and lane data, pad it slightly, and show a specific date
hypothesis: If the delivery date shown is built from actual lane and carrier performance and padded slightly, then it is usually beaten instead of missed, which builds trust instead of eroding it.

signal.check: The delivery estimate shown to customers is a vague range or the carrier's ideal SLA rather than a specific date built from real performance data.

expected_effect.size: one cited claim: a specific date lifts conversion 13% to 25% over a vague range

risk.note: A calculation and display change on PDP, cart and confirmation.

prerequisites: 90 days of delivered-minus-shipped data by lane and carrier
Handling time per SKU or warehouse
steps: Pull delivered-minus-shipped days by lane and carrier for the last 90 days.
Add handling time to get a raw estimate.
Pad the estimate slightly so it is usually beaten, while staying competitive.
Show a specific date, not a range, on PDP, cart and confirmation.
Widen the pad for a specific lane if it starts missing, not for all lanes.

test.method: Compute delivery estimate accuracy (F16) weekly and confirm it stays above 90%.

title: Hold delivery estimate accuracy above 90 percent, counting overdue orders as misses
hypothesis: If overdue, undelivered orders count as misses rather than pending, then delivery estimate accuracy reflects reality and stays a trustworthy number to manage against a 90% target.

signal.check: Delivery estimate accuracy is not tracked, or overdue undelivered orders are excluded from the calculation as pending.

expected_effect.size: target above 90%, one vendor case above 95%

risk.note: A measurement fix.

prerequisites: Delivery promise and delivered timestamps per order
steps: Compute DEA as orders delivered within promise divided by orders whose promise window has closed.
Count any overdue, undelivered order as a miss, not pending.
Track DEA weekly.
If DEA falls below 90% for 2 weeks, widen the pad for the failing lane only.

test.method: Track DEA weekly for 2 months to confirm it holds above 90%.

title: Make cutting WISMO tickets under 5 percent of orders the first post-purchase fix
hypothesis: If WISMO reduction is tackled before any other post-purchase project, then the largest and easiest-to-remove support cost driver gets cleared first, unlocking the rest of the roadmap.

signal.check: WISMO tickets are at or above 5% of orders shipped, or the rate is not being measured at all.

expected_effect.size: bands: under 3% healthy, 3% to 8% normal but expensive, above 8% structural

risk.note: A measurement and prioritization step, feeding the 3-message flow and tracking page work.

steps: Tag every support ticket as WISMO or not.
Compute WISMO tickets per order shipped monthly.
If above 5%, prioritize the 3-message flow and branded tracking page work ahead of other CX projects.
Re-measure monthly until under 5%, then under 3% for the healthy band.

test.method: Track WISMO per order monthly until it holds under 5%.

title: Add product-specific education to shipping-window messages for considered or routine-based products
hypothesis: If prep steps, first-use expectations and a realistic results timeline are added to the wait-period messages, then post-purchase dissonance drops instead of leaving the customer with silence until delivery.

signal.check: Shipping-window messages contain only tracking information with no product education, for a considered or routine-based category.

risk.note: A content addition to existing flow messages.

prerequisites: Product usage cadence and realistic timeline data
steps: Identify considered or routine-based products where a wait exists before results.
Write prep steps, what to expect on first use, and a realistic timeline to results.
Keep every claim as accurate as the product detail page.
Sequence the last message before delivery to set up the unboxing as the peak.

test.method: Track return rate for misuse-related reasons before and after adding education.

does_not_apply_when: Simple commodity reorders with nothing to explain

title: Keep transactional emails focused on the order; route cross-sell to marketing sends only
hypothesis: If tracking information stays first in transactional emails with no promotional cross-sell above it, then the customer gets what they opened the email for without feeling sold to.

signal.check: A shipping or tracking email leads with or interrupts the tracking information with promotional cross-sell content.

risk.note: A content reordering edit.

steps: Audit shipping and tracking emails for promotional content above the tracking link.
Move any cross-sell content below the order status.
Route bigger promotional pushes to permitted marketing sends instead.
Keep recommendations on the tracking page, not the email body.

test.method: Compare click-through on the tracking link before and after the reorder.

title: Reach out proactively before the customer asks when a parcel stalls or an issue is detected
hypothesis: If the brand contacts the customer first when tracking shows a stalled or delayed parcel, then WISMO contacts drop and the customer experiences the brand as on top of the problem instead of hiding from it.

signal.check: No alert exists for a stalled or delayed shipment; customers find out only by contacting support.

risk.note: Requires a tracking data feed with delay detection.

steps: Set a rule to flag a shipment with no scan update for a set number of days.
Trigger an automatic outreach message with the fact, the fix and the new timing.
Route flagged cases to a human for anything beyond a standard delay.
Track how many delays are caught proactively versus reported by the customer.

test.method: Track the share of delay cases caught proactively versus customer-reported over 60 days.

title: Choose the update channel by audience: SMS for older or US buyers, WhatsApp for opted-in India
hypothesis: If update channel is chosen by audience age and geography, then messages get opened at a higher rate because they arrive where that audience actually reads them.

signal.check: Post-purchase updates go out on one default channel regardless of the audience's age profile or geography.

expected_effect.size: one cited dataset shows automated WhatsApp journeys at 11.12% CTR versus 2.6% for broadcasts

risk.note: Requires WhatsApp Business opt-in compliance for Indian audiences.

prerequisites: WhatsApp Business opt-in in place for India, or SMS capability for other markets
[web check: WhatsApp Business opt-in rules for transactional vs marketing messages in India]
steps: Segment the audience by age skew and geography.
Use SMS for older or less digital, or US-based audiences.
Use WhatsApp journeys for Indian D2C audiences with opt-in already in place.
Check current WhatsApp Business opt-in rules before launch.

test.method: Compare open and click rate by channel for the same message type over 30 days.

title: Tell customers up front when a multi-item order will ship in separate parcels
hypothesis: If customers are told at confirmation that their order will ship in separate parcels, and each parcel gets its own tracking update, then a partial delivery does not read as a mistake.

signal.check: Multi-item orders sometimes ship in separate parcels with no advance notice and only one combined tracking status shown.

risk.note: A confirmation content and tracking-page logic change.

prerequisites: Fulfillment system data on split shipments
steps: Detect at confirmation time whether an order will ship as multiple parcels.
Add a line to the confirmation stating this up front.
Send a separate tracking update per parcel rather than one combined status.
Confirm the tracking page can show multiple parcel statuses.

test.method: Track WISMO tickets tagged as 'partial delivery confusion' before and after.

title: Give customers a short self-service window to edit the delivery address or cancel before an order ships
hypothesis: If customers can edit their address or cancel within a stated short window before shipping, then fewer mis-shipped orders and support tickets happen because the fix comes from the customer, not a support agent.

signal.check: There is no customer-facing way to edit an address or cancel an order before it ships; every change requires a support contact.

risk.note: Requires order-management system support for post-order edits within a cutoff.

prerequisites: Order management system with an editable pre-fulfillment window
steps: Define the window before an order enters fulfillment where edits are possible.
Build or enable a self-service address-edit and cancel option within that window.
State the window clearly in the order confirmation.
Route any edit request after the window closes to standard support.

test.method: Track address-correction and cancellation tickets before and after the self-service option launches.

title: Point every tracking link to a branded page on the brand's own domain, never the carrier's page
hypothesis: If the tracking link goes to a branded page instead of the carrier's page, then the highest-frequency post-purchase visit stays with the brand instead of handing it to a page that may show competitor ads.

signal.check: The tracking link in shipping emails currently points to the carrier's own tracking page.

expected_effect.size: one source claims 23% to 31% higher repeat purchase from branded tracking, a vendor claim

risk.note: Requires a tracking-page vendor or a built branded page; low risk since the carrier link can stay as a fallback.

prerequisites: Carrier API or webhook access for tracking data
steps: Shortlist a branded tracking-page vendor or build option.
Point every tracking link in confirmation and shipping messages to the branded page.
Keep the carrier link as a fallback line in the message for 30 days in case the page fails.
Confirm the page loads correctly for every carrier used.

test.method: Track click-through to the branded page and repeat purchase rate for its visitors after 90 days.

title: Build the branded tracking page with status, a recommendation, loyalty link and a clear returns path
hypothesis: If the tracking page shows status, 1 complementary recommendation, a loyalty link and a clear returns path, then the page does more than answer 'where is my order,' it also supports the next purchase.

signal.check: The branded or carrier tracking page shows only status with no recommendation, loyalty link or returns path.

risk.note: A page content build within the tracking vendor or custom page.

prerequisites: [web check: vendor features, Shopify compatibility, pricing]
steps: Add order status, estimated delivery window and carrier to the page.
Add brand logo and colors for recognition.
Add 1 complementary product recommendation.
Add a loyalty program link and a clear returns path.
Optionally add order lookup, education content, or a social feed.

test.method: Track recommendation click-through and linked purchases from the page after 60 days.

title: Instrument tracking-page recommendation clicks and linked orders separately from raw page visits
hypothesis: If recommendation clicks and the orders they lead to are tracked separately from total page visits, then the page's real revenue contribution is visible instead of assumed from visit counts alone.

signal.check: The tracking page reports only visit counts, with no click-through or linked-order tracking on its recommendation.

risk.note: An analytics tagging step.

prerequisites: Tracking page with a recommendation module
steps: Add click tracking to the recommendation module.
Attribute any resulting order back to the tracking-page click.
Report recommendation click rate and linked orders separately from raw visits.
Review monthly alongside WISMO rate.

test.method: Compare linked-order revenue against raw visit count to see whether visits alone were misleading.

title: Map the top 10 pre-purchase objections and answer them on the product page
hypothesis: If the top 10 objections from tickets, reviews and chat are answered directly on the product page, then fewer post-purchase tickets and returns happen because the question got answered before the sale, not after.

signal.check: Common post-purchase support questions and return reasons are not yet mapped back to product page content.

risk.note: A content addition to product pages; requires ticket and review data.

steps: Pull the top objections from tickets, reviews and chat: fit, results timeline, price comparison, assembly, and similar.
Rank them and pick the top 10.
Write clear answers into the product page content.
Set a standing loop: route new unanswered chat and support questions back into PDP content.

test.method: Track return rate and ticket volume for the addressed objections over 90 days.

title: Show landed cost before checkout on cross-border orders, not as a delivery surprise
hypothesis: If duties, taxes and customs fees are shown before checkout on cross-border orders, then customers do not get an unpleasant surprise at delivery that damages trust and drives refusal or WISMO contacts.

signal.check: Cross-border orders show only the product price at checkout, with duties or customs fees appearing only at delivery.

risk.note: Requires landed-cost calculation at checkout, which may need a vendor or platform feature.

prerequisites: Duty and tax calculation capability at checkout
steps: Confirm which ship-to countries incur duties, taxes or customs fees.
Add landed cost display before the final checkout step.
Add customs status to the branded tracking page.
Check returns and refund law per market before finalizing the display language.

test.method: Track checkout completion rate and WISMO contacts about surprise fees before and after.

does_not_apply_when: Domestic-only stores with no cross-border shipping

title: Design the unboxing experience on purpose, as the journey's main peak
hypothesis: If unboxing is designed on purpose instead of left to a bare box, then the brand controls its one physical touchpoint and its natural peak-end moment instead of leaving it to chance.

signal.check: The current unboxing is a bare box with no deliberate reveal, insert or brand moment planned into it.

risk.note: A packaging and fulfillment change; test with a small batch first.

steps: Write the brand's one-line promise to guide material choice.
Design a layered reveal: outer box, tissue or wrap, insert, product.
Add 1 standard insert and 1 script-breaking surprise element.
Walk a live order end to end before rolling out at scale.

test.method: Track unboxing UGC volume and review rate for 90 days after launch.

does_not_apply_when: Commodity or marketplace-heavy catalogues where the brand does not control the unboxing moment

title: Give every order a standard insert and reserve handwritten notes for VIP or high-value orders
hypothesis: If every order gets a standard thank-you insert and handwritten notes go only to VIP or high-value orders, then the personal touch stays real at the top tier without breaking the budget at full volume.

signal.check: Every order currently gets the same insert with no tiering by order value, or handwritten notes are attempted at full volume.

expected_effect.size: one source cites about 80% of brands add at least 1 packaging customization

risk.note: A fulfillment process change.

prerequisites: Order value data to define the VIP or high-value threshold
steps: Design 1 standard insert: thank you, and a QR to a how-to video or loyalty signup.
Set a threshold for VIP or high-value orders.
Reserve handwritten (or item-specific merge field) notes for orders above that threshold.
Add an unexpected small gift where the order type allows.

test.method: Track review rate and repeat rate for VIP-tier orders receiving notes against the standard tier.

title: Cap packaging spend at 2 to 5 percent of product cost and model insert cost at current order volume
hypothesis: If packaging spend is capped as a percentage of product cost and insert cost is modeled at current order volume, then unboxing spend stays disciplined instead of creeping up per-order.

signal.check: Packaging or insert spend has not been checked against product cost as a percentage, or has never been modeled at current monthly order volume.

expected_effect.size: bands: a branded moment under $0.50 per order, full premium $2.80 to $4.50

risk.note: A budgeting check.

steps: Compute current packaging cost as a percentage of product cost.
Set the target band at 2% to 5% of product cost.
Model insert cost per order times orders per month to see total monthly cost.
If the insert stack exceeds the band at volume, drop the lowest-value insert first, never the first-use guide.

test.method: Recompute the packaging cost percentage after any insert change.

title: Layer the unboxing reveal and add a first-use guide with a QR to a short setup video
hypothesis: If the box, tissue, wrap and insert are layered on purpose and paired with a QR to a 60-second setup video, then the reveal builds anticipation and reduces first-use confusion in the same moment.

signal.check: The current box opens straight to the product with no layering and no first-use guidance.

risk.note: A packaging design change.

steps: Layer the box: outer box, tissue or wrap, insert, product.
Add 1 script-breaking surprise element.
Include a first-use guide with a QR code to a short setup video.
Test the full sequence with a live order.

test.method: Track return rate for setup-confusion reasons before and after adding the guide.

title: Match packaging materials and texture to the brand's one-line promise
hypothesis: If packaging weight, rigidity and texture are chosen to match the brand's stated promise, then the physical experience confirms the brand story instead of contradicting it within milliseconds of opening.

signal.check: Packaging materials have not been checked against the brand's one-line promise for a mismatch, such as premium materials on a 'natural' brand or flimsy materials on a 'premium' brand.

risk.note: A materials review, potentially followed by a packaging update.

steps: Write the brand's one-line promise.
Walk a live order and note the weight, rigidity and texture of every touch.
Flag any material that reads as contradicting the promise, for example premium tactile packaging on a natural-positioned brand.
Swap the conflicting material for one that matches.

test.method: Re-walk a live order after the swap and confirm no conflicting signal remains.

title: Put an unconditional gift in the box, never a conditional discount code
hypothesis: If the box gift is unconditional, unadvertised and has no code or minimum-spend requirement, then it reads as generosity instead of training the customer to wait for the next markdown.

signal.check: The current box 'gift' is really a discount code with a minimum spend, review or referral condition attached.

risk.note: A fulfillment and budgeting change; budget the gift inside COGS.

prerequisites: Budget allocated inside COGS for the gift
steps: Remove any conditional code framed as a gift.
Choose a relevant, unadvertised item to include instead.
Budget the gift cost inside COGS against retention, not as a marketing expense.
Match the gift's perceived value and relevance to the order.

test.method: Compare repeat rate for gift recipients against a matched control group without the gift.

title: Make handwritten notes item-specific, honestly produced, and never falsely claimed as staff-written
hypothesis: If notes reference the exact item, use a real signature or item-specific merge field, and are never falsely claimed as personally handwritten when a machine wrote them, then the personal touch stays credible instead of becoming a trust risk if discovered.

signal.check: Notes going into orders are generic form letters, or a machine-written note is being represented to customers as personally handwritten.

risk.note: Requires either a robotic handwriting vendor or a real-signature production process; verify vendor claims before adopting.

prerequisites: Trigger list: high-value first purchase, subscription anniversary, VIP appreciation, resolved failure
[web check: robotic handwriting vendor pen and paper quality, integrations]
steps: Define the triggers: high-value first purchase, subscription anniversary, VIP appreciation, a resolved failure.
Write the note to reference the exact item purchased.
