Use a real signature or an item-specific merge field, never a form letter.
If using a robotic vendor, evaluate pen and paper quality first and never claim staff wrote it if asked.
Follow up a few days later with a short 'did it work' check-in.

test.method: Track retention for note recipients against a matched group without a note, and confirm no customer complaint about a fake handwritten claim.

title: Avoid a cheap, irrelevant or clearance gift that reads as landfill
hypothesis: If any box gift is checked for relevance and perceived value before inclusion, then it reads as a thoughtful extra instead of clearance stock dumped in the box.

signal.check: A gift being considered for inclusion is leftover clearance stock with no clear relevance to the order.

risk.note: A selection criterion, low cost to apply.

steps: List candidate gift items being considered.
Score each for relevance to the order and perceived value.
Reject any item that is purely clearance stock with no relevance.
Test 1 gift on a small batch before including it at full volume.

test.method: Watch for any customer feedback describing the gift as confusing or unwanted.

title: Treat packaging as a filmable creative asset and track unboxing UGC volume as its own metric
hypothesis: If packaging is designed to be filmed and unboxing UGC volume is tracked and reposted, then the unboxing spend earns its keep as a content asset, not just a one-time customer moment.

signal.check: Unboxing UGC is not being tracked or actively captured and reposted despite packaging spend.

risk.note: A tracking and content-capture process, using the existing packaging.

prerequisites: Social listening or a branded hashtag
steps: Set up a branded hashtag or tag prompt for unboxing content.
Track unboxing UGC volume monthly.
Ask permission and repost strong UGC across channels.
Treat rising UGC volume as the metric for this spend, not just review rate.

test.method: Track monthly unboxing UGC volume for 90 days.

title: Offer gift wrap and a hidden-price gift receipt at checkout for orders marked as a gift
hypothesis: If gift wrap and a gift receipt with the price hidden are offered at checkout for orders marked as a gift, then gift-givers get a smoother experience that can lift conversion on gift occasions.

signal.check: There is no gift-wrap or hidden-price gift-receipt option at checkout.

risk.note: A checkout feature addition; check platform or app support.

prerequisites: Checkout platform support for a gift option or a compatible app
steps: Add a 'this is a gift' checkbox at checkout.
Offer gift wrap as an add-on where feasible.
Generate a packing slip and box with the price hidden for gift orders.
Test around a gifting season first.

test.method: Track gift-option uptake and AOV for gift-marked orders after launch.

title: Trigger a product education sequence about 48 hours after delivery confirmation
hypothesis: If a quick-start guide, video tutorial and common-mistakes tip send about 48 hours after delivery, then misuse-related returns drop and the customer gets more comfortable with the product sooner.

signal.check: No education sequence sends after delivery, or it sends on a fixed calendar date instead of tied to the delivery event.

expected_effect.size: one Klaviyo case reports 44.5% open, 2.81% click on an education flow

risk.note: A flow build in the existing ESP.

prerequisites: Genuine post-purchase tips per top 3 product categories
steps: Pick the top 3 categories by order share.
Trigger the sequence at delivery confirmation plus about 48 hours, sooner for complex products.
Include a quick-start guide, video tutorial and common mistakes.
Include 1 tip not already on the product page.

test.method: Track return rate for misuse reasons and open and click rates for 90 days after launch.

title: Send a reassurance message about 2 days after purchase
hypothesis: If a short 'you made the right choice' message sends about 2 days after purchase, then post-purchase doubt gets addressed early instead of left to build during the wait.

signal.check: No reassurance-toned message currently sends in the first few days after purchase.

expected_effect.size: one Klaviyo case reports 47.4% open for a subscription brand

risk.note: A flow build.

steps: Write a short, reassurance-toned subject line and message.
Trigger it about 2 days after purchase.
Keep the tone warm, not salesy.
Track open rate against the flow average.

test.method: Compare open rate for the reassurance message against the ESP's average automation open rate.

title: Ask for honest, unfiltered reviews across the post-purchase flow, thank-you page and insert
hypothesis: If review requests go to every customer, not just ones likely to be satisfied, and ask for specific use cases, then the review base stays trustworthy and useful instead of gamed.

signal.check: Review requests are filtered to send only to customers flagged as satisfied, or reviews are not requested at multiple touchpoints.

risk.note: A policy and flow change; never fabricate or gate reviews.

steps: Remove any filter that sends review requests only to satisfied buyers.
Ask for specific use cases and outcomes in the request copy.
Add the request to the post-purchase flow, thank-you page and packaging insert.
Never fabricate or gate reviews, even where third-party content may influence AI recommendations.

test.method: Track review volume and rating distribution for 90 days after removing the filter.

title: Give subscriptions real flexibility to change cadence, skip, or pause
hypothesis: If subscribers can change cadence, skip or pause instead of only cancel, then fewer subscriptions end outright and fewer chargebacks come from a rigid plan.

signal.check: The subscription program only offers cancel, with no skip, pause or cadence-change option.

risk.note: A subscription platform feature change.

prerequisites: Subscription management platform with skip/pause support
steps: Confirm the subscription platform supports skip, pause and cadence change.
Add self-service controls for all 3 options.
Promote the flexibility in account and cancellation-flow messaging.
Track churn rate for subscribers who use skip or pause versus those who do not.

test.method: Track subscription churn rate 90 days after adding flexibility options.

title: Offer a post-checkout upsell framed as completing the purchase, not new selling
hypothesis: If a larger size or adjacent item is offered right after checkout and framed as completing the purchase, then AOV rises with low friction because the customer has already committed to buy.

signal.check: No post-checkout upsell offer exists between order confirmation and the thank-you page.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no lift quantified in the source

risk.note: A checkout or post-checkout page addition; low friction since order is already placed.

prerequisites: Checkout platform support for a post-purchase upsell page or app
steps: Pick 1 low-friction upsell: a larger size or an adjacent item.
Frame the offer as completing the purchase, not as a new sale.
Place it on the post-checkout or thank-you page.
Track acceptance rate and AOV lift.

test.method: Track AOV and upsell acceptance rate for 30 days after launch.

title: Extend education into an always-on AI assistant only where the brand has real repeat-need expertise
hypothesis: If an always-on assistant is built only for setup, usage, troubleshooting and replenishment in a category where the brand has genuine expertise, then it earns its keep on retention and repeat, not novelty.

signal.check: An AI assistant is being considered mainly as a support-deflection tool rather than for genuine post-purchase help in a category the brand knows deeply.

expected_effect.size: forecast, 1 source, no performance data attached

risk.note: New customer-facing AI tooling; test on a narrow use case before wide rollout.

prerequisites: Helpdesk or chat platform with AI support
steps: Confirm the brand has real expertise in the category, not just a general FAQ.
Scope the assistant to setup, usage, troubleshooting and replenishment advice.
Measure it by retention and repeat rate, not chat volume alone.
[web check: current AI support tool capabilities and pricing]

test.method: Compare repeat rate for assistant users against matched non-users after 90 days.

does_not_apply_when: Categories where the brand has no genuine repeat-need expertise to hand to the bot

title: Show a pause, skip or discount offer at the subscription cancel step before it completes
hypothesis: If a pause, skip or discount offer appears before a cancellation completes, then some subscribers who would have churned stay instead, without making cancellation itself hard to find.

signal.check: The cancel flow completes immediately with no pause, skip or discount offer shown first.

risk.note: A cancel-flow UX change; must not make cancellation itself hard to complete.

prerequisites: Subscription platform support for a save-offer step
steps: Add a pause, skip or discount offer screen before the cancellation confirms.
Keep the actual cancel option clearly available and easy to complete.
Route anyone who declines the offer into the cancelled cohort for win-back.
Track save-offer acceptance rate.

test.method: Track cancellation completion rate and save-offer acceptance for 60 days.

title: Collapse the refund timeline and measure request-to-initiation and initiation-to-receipt separately
hypothesis: If the refund process moves from the traditional 10 to 14 days toward hours or minutes, and both timing legs are measured separately, then returners repeat at a rate that matches or beats non-returners instead of leaving for good.

signal.check: Refund cycle time is not measured, or takes multiple days with no split between request-to-initiation and initiation-to-receipt.

expected_effect.size: vendor cases claim faster refunds paired with higher repeat purchase, no shared methodology

risk.note: Faster refunds raise fraud exposure; measure return-fraud losses before scaling (paired idea).

prerequisites: Return request, approval and refund timestamps
[web check: returns and refunds law per ship-to market]
steps: Measure refund_cycle_days (request to receipt) and refund_initiation_days (request to initiation) separately.
Shortlist a returns or payments vendor for faster refunds.
Pilot on a limited market or order value first.
Compare returners' 60-day repurchase rate against non-returners after the pilot.

test.method: Compute the gap between returner and non-returner repeat rate after the pilot.

title: Offer a clear choice between refund to original payment and store credit, never silent substitution
hypothesis: If the customer always gets a clear choice between original-payment refund and store credit, then trust holds instead of eroding when credit is silently substituted to protect revenue.

signal.check: Store credit is issued by default without offering the customer a clear choice of original-payment refund.

risk.note: A returns-flow policy and interface change.

prerequisites: Returns platform or process with refund-method selection
steps: Add a clear choice screen: refund to original payment or store credit.
Remove any default that silently issues credit instead of a refund.
Train support staff to always offer both options.
Track how many customers choose each option.

test.method: Check for any customer complaint about a forced or silent credit substitution over 60 days.

title: Measure fraud losses and cash-flow impact before scaling faster or instant refunds
hypothesis: If return-fraud rate and cash-flow impact are measured before scaling instant refunds, then the speed gain does not come with a hidden fraud cost the business only discovers later.

signal.check: Faster or instant refunds are being scaled with no measurement of fraud rate or cash position.

risk.note: A monitoring step; the risk is in skipping it, not in doing it.

steps: Measure current return-fraud rate before any refund-speed change.
Measure cash-flow impact of refunding faster.
Run the faster-refund test on a limited cohort first (paired idea).
Only scale if fraud losses and cash impact stay inside the brand's set tolerance.

test.method: Compare fraud rate and cash impact between the instant-refund cohort and the standard cohort.
test.read_point: At the end of the pilot

title: Give returners a self-service portal with keep-it-or-donate refunds for low-value items
hypothesis: If returners get a self-service portal and low-value items are refunded without needing a return shipment, then the return experience gets faster and cheaper at the same time.

signal.check: Returns require a support ticket to initiate, with no self-service option and no keep-it-or-donate refund path for low-value items.

risk.note: A returns platform or app addition.

prerequisites: A defined low-value threshold for keep-it refunds
steps: Set up a self-service returns portal.
Set a low-value threshold below which a refund issues without requiring the item back.
Offer exchange, credit and refund options clearly in the portal.
Track ticket volume for return-related contacts before and after.

test.method: Compare return-related ticket volume 60 days before and after launch.

title: Publish the returns policy where shoppers see it before buying, checked against law per market
hypothesis: If the returns policy is visible on the product page and footer before purchase, and checked against law in every ship-to market, then fewer purchases stall on an unanswered returns question.

signal.check: The returns policy is hard to find before checkout, or has not been checked against consumer protection law in a ship-to market.

expected_effect.size: one source cites 67% of shoppers check the returns policy before buying

risk.note: A content placement and legal-check step.

prerequisites: [web check: returns and refund law per ship-to market]
steps: Add a clear returns-policy link to the product page and footer.
Check the policy against consumer protection and refund law in every ship-to market.
Update the policy before any change goes live.
Re-check the law before every future policy change.

test.method: Track PDP-to-cart conversion before and after making the policy more visible.

title: Gate further returns work on returners' repeat rate matching or beating non-returners
hypothesis: If returns and refund investment continues only while the returner repeat gap stays healthy, then the team knows exactly when returns work has done its job and effort can move to the next roadmap step.

signal.check: Returns and refund process investment is ongoing with no check of whether returners now repeat at the same rate as non-returners.

risk.note: A gate check on an existing workstream.

prerequisites: Return request, approval and refund timestamps
Repeat purchase data for returners and non-returners
steps: Compute returner_repeat_rate_90 and non_returner_repeat_rate_90.
Compute the gap between the two.
Continue returns investment while the gap is negative.
Move on to the next roadmap step once the gap reaches zero or above.

test.method: Recompute the gap monthly until it clears zero.

title: Track return-to-origin rate for COD orders and confirm high-risk orders before dispatch
hypothesis: If return-to-origin rate is tracked as its own cost line and high-RTO lanes or first-time COD customers get a confirmation call or WhatsApp message before dispatch, then wasted shipping and handling cost on undeliverable COD orders drops.

signal.check: Cash-on-delivery orders are dispatched with no RTO tracking and no pre-dispatch confirmation step for high-risk lanes or first-time customers.

risk.note: A pre-dispatch process addition; requires a call or WhatsApp confirmation capability.

prerequisites: COD order data with lane and customer history
Call center or WhatsApp confirmation capability
steps: Track RTO rate by lane and flag high-RTO lanes.
Flag first-time COD customers separately.
Add a confirmation call or WhatsApp message before dispatch for flagged orders.
Track RTO rate for confirmed versus unconfirmed orders.

test.method: Compare RTO rate for confirmed versus unconfirmed high-risk orders over 60 days.

does_not_apply_when: Stores that do not offer cash on delivery

title: Track chargebacks and payment disputes as their own cost line, separate from returns and refunds
hypothesis: If chargebacks and disputes get their own count and dollar total instead of being folded into returns, then the real cost of payment disputes becomes visible and can be managed on its own.

signal.check: Chargebacks and payment disputes are not tracked separately from returns and refunds, or not tracked at all.

risk.note: A reporting build using existing payment processor data.

steps: Pull chargeback and dispute count and dollar total from the payment processor.
Report it as its own line, separate from returns and refunds.
Report it alongside the support cost-per-contact baseline (F19).
Review monthly for trend.

test.method: Track chargeback count and dollar total monthly for one quarter.

title: Reduce effort in every service moment: one-touch resolution, no repeat explanations, no dark patterns
hypothesis: If service moments like returns, WISMO and complaints are resolved in one touch with no repeat explanations or dark patterns, then customers become less disloyal, since high-effort interactions drive disloyalty far more than low-effort ones.

signal.check: Resolving a return, a WISMO contact or a complaint currently requires multiple touches, repeated explanations, or an escalation for a routine refund.

expected_effect.size: one cited study found 96% of high-effort customers became more disloyal versus 9% of low-effort ones

risk.note: A support process redesign; low execution risk since it removes steps rather than adding them.

prerequisites: Support ticket log with resolution-touch count
steps: Walk a return and a WISMO contact as a customer to feel the current effort level.
Remove any requirement to repeat information already given.
Give refunds without escalation for standard cases.
Remove any dark pattern: hidden cancel flows, forced logins, repeated forms.

test.method: Track first-contact resolution rate and CSAT for service-moment tickets over 60 days.

title: Over-recover every genuine service failure with a scoped human gesture
hypothesis: If every genuine failure (wrong item, late parcel, damaged box) gets a refund without escalation plus a scoped human gesture, then a bad recovery, which costs more than a good one gains, gets avoided.

signal.check: A genuine service failure was handled with only the minimum required fix and no human gesture, or with escalation the customer had to push for.

risk.note: A support policy addition; scope it to real failures only, not a routine cost.

prerequisites: Support ticket log tagged by failure type
steps: Confirm the case is a genuine failure, not a manufactured one.
Refund without escalation.
Offer to let the customer keep or donate the product where sensible.
Add a scoped human gesture and replace same-day where feasible.
Log the case in the failure cohort for tracking.

test.method: Track first-contact resolution, CSAT and 90-day repeat rate for the failure cohort.

title: Give frontline support agents authority for one-time exceptions on sympathetic cases
hypothesis: If frontline agents can approve a one-time exception beyond policy for a sympathetic case without escalating, then the customer gets resolved fast instead of waiting on a manager for a small exception.

signal.check: Every exception to policy currently requires manager approval, with no standing authority given to frontline agents.

risk.note: A policy and authority-level change.

prerequisites: Support team and manager buy-in on the authority limit
steps: Define the scope of a one-time exception agents can approve without escalation.
Set a dollar or scope cap on the exception.
Train agents on when to use it.
Review a sample of exceptions monthly for consistency.

test.method: Track first-reply and resolution time for exception cases before and after.

title: Build a staff checklist for known edge cases before they happen
hypothesis: If a checklist exists for known edge cases (customs holds, mis-shipped items, stockouts after confirmation, failed subscription payments) before they happen, then agents follow a plan instead of improvising live on a ticket.

signal.check: There is no written checklist for common edge cases; agents handle each one from scratch.

risk.note: A documentation exercise, done ahead of live tickets.

prerequisites: List of past edge cases from ticket history
steps: List known edge cases: an order stuck in customs, a mis-shipped item, a stockout after confirmation, a subscription payment failure.
Write the standard response and fix for each during journey mapping, not live on a ticket.
Share the checklist with the support team.
Update it as new edge cases appear.

test.method: Track resolution time and consistency for edge-case tickets before and after the checklist exists.

title: Track first-contact resolution, CSAT and repeat rate for the customer failure cohort separately
hypothesis: If customers who had a genuine failure are tracked as their own cohort for resolution speed, satisfaction and repeat rate, then recovery quality gets measured directly instead of assumed.

signal.check: There is no separate tracked cohort for customers who experienced a service failure.

risk.note: A reporting build.

prerequisites: Support ticket log tagged by failure type
steps: Tag every order that had a genuine service failure.
Build the failure cohort in the reporting system.
Track first-contact resolution, CSAT and 90-day repeat rate for this cohort.
Compare against customers with no failure as a benchmark.

test.method: Review the failure cohort's metrics monthly.

title: Weight 'helped me when something went wrong' above generic friendliness when prioritizing CX fixes
hypothesis: If problem-resolution quality is weighted above generic friendliness in CX prioritization, then budget goes to the driver shoppers say matters more, not the one that is easiest to talk about.

signal.check: CX prioritization currently ranks friendliness or tone above how well a real problem gets resolved.

expected_effect.size: one informal webinar poll ranked problem resolution third, ahead of product, behind corporate attitude and ease of doing business

risk.note: A prioritization framework adjustment.

prerequisites: Current CX priority list or roadmap
steps: Review the current CX priority list.
Rank 'help when something goes wrong' at or near the top, above generic friendliness training.
Reallocate budget from friendliness-only initiatives to resolution-quality fixes.
Note this order may vary by category; re-check against the brand's own feedback.

test.method: Compare CSAT drivers named in customer feedback before and after the reprioritization.

title: Establish cost-per-contact and return-per-contact baselines before calling support a profit centre
hypothesis: If cost-per-contact and return-per-contact are both measured, then any claim that support pays for itself has real numbers behind it instead of a slogan.

signal.check: Support is described as a profit centre with no measured cost-per-contact or return-per-contact baseline.

expected_effect.size: unknown, direction only, no source numbers

risk.note: A measurement build using support and order data.

prerequisites: Support cost and contact count for the last 90 days
steps: Compute cost_per_contact as support cost divided by contacts for the last 90 days.
Compute return_per_contact as gross profit from orders linked to contacts divided by contacts.
Compute the profit_centre_ratio as return_per_contact divided by cost_per_contact.
Report the ratio monthly and watch whether it rises while complaints stay flat.

test.method: Track the profit_centre_ratio monthly for one quarter.

title: Resolve the support issue first, then offer 1 relevant recommendation, never before
hypothesis: If support always resolves the customer's issue before offering any product recommendation, then the recommendation lands as helpful instead of as an upsell attempt during a problem.

signal.check: Support agents or bots offer a product recommendation before the customer's original issue is resolved.

risk.note: A support script and bot-flow policy change.

prerequisites: Full order and customer history context in the support tool
steps: Update support scripts and bot flows to resolve the issue first, always.
Add 1 relevant, non-intrusive recommendation only after resolution.
Base the recommendation on individual fit, not just best-sellers.
Monitor acceptance and complaint rates on the recommendation.

test.method: Track complaint rate about upsell timing and recommendation acceptance rate for 60 days.

title: Automate high-volume, low-complexity support contacts first, keep humans for complex or emotional cases
hypothesis: If order-status and other high-volume, low-complexity contacts get automated first while complex or emotional cases stay with humans, then support capacity frees up without customers feeling stuck with a bot on a hard problem.

signal.check: Support automation is either absent or applied to everything, including emotional or complex cases that need a human.

expected_effect.size: some brands report 64% to 95% AI resolution on order-status queries, a vendor-reported figure

risk.note: A support tool configuration change; keep an easy human escalation path.

prerequisites: [web check: current AI support tool capabilities and pricing]
steps: Identify high-volume, low-complexity contact types, starting with order status.
Automate those first, with a clear and easy human escalation path.
Keep emotional or complex cases routed to a human by default.
Track resolution rate and CSAT for automated versus human-handled contacts.

test.method: Track ticket backlog and CSAT for 60 days after automating order-status contacts.

title: Write the brand's voice spec before turning on any customer-facing support bot
hypothesis: If tone, forbidden words and the brand's distinct sound are written down before a bot goes live, then the bot avoids flattening the brand into a generic support voice.

signal.check: A support bot (order status, return authorization, WISMO auto-reply) is live or planned with no written voice spec behind it.

risk.note: A documentation step before or alongside a bot rollout.

steps: Write the brand's tone in a few sentences.
List words the brand never uses.
State how the brand should sound different from a generic support bot.
Have someone who knows the brand judge bot transcripts blind against the spec.
Review for drift after every bot or model update.

test.method: Have a blind reviewer confirm they recognize the brand voice in 3 sampled transcripts.
test.read_point: Before launch and after each update

title: Keep a human voice for handwritten notes, recovery emails and VIP messages, without AI polish
hypothesis: If notes, recovery emails and VIP messages are written and left in a human voice on purpose, then the one moment meant to feel personal does not get flattened by AI polish.

signal.check: Notes, recovery emails or VIP messages are being run through AI polishing tools with no check on whether it flattens the personal tone.

expected_effect.size: claim has no test data attached in the source

risk.note: A writing-process guideline.

prerequisites: List of touchpoints meant to feel personal: notes, recovery, VIP
steps: List the touchpoints meant to feel personal.
Write those directly in the brand's human voice, skipping AI polishing tools.
Test whether removing AI polish changes customer response on 1 trust-sensitive touchpoint.
Keep AI tools for high-volume, low-personal-stakes messages instead.

test.method: Run an A/B test comparing a human-voice version against an AI-polished version on 1 recovery or note touchpoint.

title: Give AI budget to genuine post-purchase help, not only ticket deflection
hypothesis: If AI budget goes to genuine setup, troubleshooting and replenishment help instead of only deflecting tickets, then the investment builds retention, not just cost savings.

signal.check: AI support spend is justified only by ticket deflection or cost savings, with no genuine post-purchase help use case funded.

expected_effect.size: cites an unnamed study, treated as a forecast

risk.note: A budget allocation decision; only in categories with real brand expertise to encode.

prerequisites: Genuine product expertise in the category
steps: Review current AI support budget and what it is justified by.
Identify a genuine help use case: setup, troubleshooting, replenishment advice.
Allocate a portion of AI budget to that use case, not only deflection.
Measure retention and repeat rate for users of the help feature.

test.method: Compare repeat rate for genuine-help feature users against non-users after 90 days.

title: Build loyalty tiers only once delivery, returns and support are reliable
hypothesis: If loyalty tier work waits until delivery estimate accuracy, WISMO and returns are all healthy, then the program sits on a foundation that can actually support the promises it makes.

signal.check: A loyalty or VIP tier program is being planned or built while delivery estimate accuracy, WISMO rate or returner repeat gap are not yet healthy.

risk.note: A go/no-go gate on a planned program.

steps: Check DEA is above 90%.
Check WISMO is under 5% of orders.
Check the returner repeat gap is at or above zero.
Check support cost-per-contact and return-per-contact baselines exist.
Pause loyalty program work until all 4 are met.

test.method: Re-check the 4 gates monthly until all are met, then proceed to loyalty design.

title: Prefer experiential and status rewards over points-only discounts in a loyalty program
hypothesis: If loyalty rewards favor early access, events, line passes and recognition over pure point-for-discount redemption, then loyalty builds status and identity instead of training customers to wait for a deal.

signal.check: The loyalty program, if one exists, offers only points-for-discount redemption with no experiential or status rewards.

expected_effect.size: one vendor case reports 66% repeat among redeemers and a 15.4x loyalty ROI

risk.note: A loyalty program redesign; can run alongside an existing points system.

prerequisites: Loyalty platform with tier or reward configuration
steps: List current reward types in the program.
Add experiential and status rewards: early access, events, line passes, recognition, exclusive content.
De-prioritize points-only discounts as the main reward.
Track redeemer repeat rate for experiential versus discount rewards.

test.method: Compare redeemer repeat rate for experiential rewards against discount-only rewards after 90 days.

title: Integrate loyalty reward redemption into checkout and measure redeemer versus non-redeemer repeat rate
hypothesis: If reward redemption happens right inside checkout and the program is judged by redeemer versus non-redeemer repeat rate, then the loyalty program's real value becomes measurable instead of assumed.

signal.check: Loyalty rewards require a separate step outside checkout to redeem, or redeemer repeat rate is not tracked against non-redeemers.

expected_effect.size: one example reports 30% redeemer repeat versus 10% non-redeemer

risk.note: A checkout integration change.

prerequisites: Loyalty platform with a checkout integration option
steps: Integrate reward redemption directly into the checkout flow.
Remove any separate step required to redeem.
Track repeat rate and LTV separately for redeemers versus non-redeemers.
Report the comparison monthly.

test.method: Compare redeemer and non-redeemer repeat rate 90 days after integration.

title: Structure loyalty tiers around milestones and status, and message the top tier least
hypothesis: If loyalty tiers are built around milestones and status and the top tier gets the fewest, least aggressive messages, then top-tier customers feel protected and recognized instead of marketed at.

signal.check: Loyalty tiers, if they exist, are not built around clear milestones, or the top tier receives the same message frequency as everyone else.

expected_effect.size: one cited program: about 46 million members, about 80% of sales, top-tier retention near 90%, a vendor write-up

risk.note: A loyalty program structure change.

prerequisites: VIP definition from the revenue and profit concentration idea
steps: Define 3 or so tiers by milestone and status, not just spend.
Set the top tier's messaging frequency lower than lower tiers.
Protect the relationship at the top tier with no incentive pressure.
Review tier definitions yearly against the brand's own top-20% data.

test.method: Track top-tier repeat rate and message engagement 90 days after the tier restructure.

title: Re-engage lapsed customers with valuable content and segmented offers before a generic discount
hypothesis: If lapsed customers get relevant content and a segmented offer before a generic discount, then reactivation happens without training the whole base to wait for a markdown.

signal.check: The current lapsed-customer approach leads with a generic discount code with no segmentation or content step first.

expected_effect.size: one case reports a 29-point retention lift in 30 days from a segmented, non-discount sequence

risk.note: A flow and segmentation build.

prerequisites: Content or product update relevant to that segment
steps: Define the lapsed segment.
Build a content-first message before any discount.
Segment the offer by what is relevant to that group, not a blanket code.
Track reactivation rate against the prior generic-discount approach.

test.method: Compare reactivation rate for the segmented approach against the prior generic discount over 30 days.

title: Build community only where a real shared activity already exists
hypothesis: If community is built only around a genuine shared activity (a run club, a restock alert group, a top-spender chat), then it becomes a retention channel competitors cannot copy instead of an empty tab.

signal.check: A generic 'community' feature or tab is planned or live with no real shared activity behind it.

expected_effect.size: no measured outcome attached in any source; examples only

risk.note: A resourcing decision; an empty community feature has real ongoing maintenance cost.

prerequisites: A genuine shared activity or interest identified among top customers
steps: Identify whether a real shared activity exists: a run club, restock alerts, a top-spender chat.
If none exists, do not launch a generic community feature.
If one exists, build the community channel around that specific activity.
Track engagement and repeat rate for community members versus matched non-members.

test.method: Compare repeat rate for community members against matched non-members after 6 months.

does_not_apply_when: No real shared activity exists among the customer base

title: Audit the lapsed list for unresolved service issues before sending any win-back campaign
hypothesis: If the lapsed list is checked for open tickets, returns or 1-star reviews before a win-back send, then the campaign does not fire into unresolved problems that a discount cannot fix.

signal.check: A win-back campaign is planned or running with no audit of the lapsed list for open tickets, returns or 1-star reviews.

risk.note: A pre-send audit step.

prerequisites: Support ticket, return and review data
steps: Pull the lapsed list.
Check the share with an open ticket, a return, or a 1-star review.
If above 20%, fix the underlying experience issue before sending win-back.
Proceed with the win-back send only once the share is under 20%.

test.method: Recheck the lapsed list's issue share before every win-back send.

title: Time win-back off the customer's RFM cadence, or 30 to 45 days after last purchase where RFM is not available
hypothesis: If win-back triggers off RFM At Risk status where the data exists, and off a 30 to 45 day window otherwise, then the message reaches the customer near their actual drop-off point instead of a fixed 90-plus day default.

signal.check: Win-back triggers off a fixed day count (commonly 90 days or more) with no RFM-based option even where order history supports it.

expected_effect.size: one cited Klaviyo benchmark reports 2.3x better conversion at 30 to 45 days versus 90 plus

risk.note: A flow trigger change.

prerequisites: Order history depth to support RFM
steps: Check whether enough order history exists to use RFM At Risk as the trigger.
If yes, trigger win-back off RFM At Risk.
If not, trigger 30 to 45 days after the last purchase instead of 90 plus.
Never use one fixed day count across every customer.

test.method: Compare win-back conversion rate for the new trigger against the old fixed-day trigger.

title: Escalate the win-back incentive across the sequence instead of leading with a flat discount
hypothesis: If a win-back sequence starts with no discount, then rises through 10%, 15% and free shipping, then it converts better than one flat discount because escalation matches urgency to lapse length.

signal.check: The win-back sequence leads with the same flat discount in every message instead of escalating.

expected_effect.size: one cited claim: escalation beats a flat discount by 34%

risk.note: A sequence and offer rebuild.

steps: Rebuild the sequence: message 1 with no discount, message 2 at 10%, message 3 at 15%, message 4 with free shipping.
Space messages to match the brand's typical decision window.
Track reactivation rate at each step.
Stop escalation once the customer converts.

test.method: Compare reactivation rate for the escalating sequence against the old flat-discount sequence.

title: Segment win-back by the reason for lapse and measure recovery separately per reason
hypothesis: If win-back is segmented by reason for lapse (price, experience, product gap) and measured separately, then the message matches the actual reason the customer left instead of one generic reactivation offer.

signal.check: Win-back sends the same message and offer to every lapsed customer regardless of why they stopped buying.

expected_effect.size: bands cited: 12% to 20% average reactivation, 20% to 35% top quartile

risk.note: A segmentation and messaging build.

prerequisites: A way to infer lapse reason: survey, support tickets, price-sensitivity signals
steps: Group lapsed customers by likely reason: price, experience issue, or product gap.
Write a distinct message per reason group.
Measure reactivation rate, revenue recovered, and 90-day repeat rate separately per group.
Refine the reason grouping based on which segment performs best.

test.method: Compare reactivation rate and 90-day repeat rate across lapse-reason segments.

title: Test retention structure and timing before offers, and offers before messaging
hypothesis: If retention tests always start with structure and timing, then offers, then messaging last, then the highest-leverage changes get tested first instead of a subject-line tweak standing in for real strategy.

signal.check: The current test backlog is mostly subject-line, timing or copy tests with no structural or offer-level tests planned.

risk.note: A test-planning process change.

prerequisites: Named retention constraint (F1, F2 or F3)
steps: List all planned or running retention tests.
Reclassify each as structure and timing, offer, or messaging.
Reorder the backlog to run structure and timing tests first, then offers, then messaging.
Keep 1 person accountable for retention strategy and profitability across executors.

test.method: Check whether the top of the test backlog matches the priority order after 1 planning cycle.

title: Build the post-purchase roadmap in payoff order with a named exit gate for each step
hypothesis: If the roadmap moves through delivery accuracy, returns, unboxing, nudges, quiz, loyalty, gifts and win-back in that order with a gate per step, then a later step never gets funded while an earlier gate is still unmet.

signal.check: Post-purchase projects are being worked in no particular order, or a later step (like loyalty) is funded while an earlier gate (like WISMO) is still unmet.

risk.note: A planning and governance step.

prerequisites: Current values for WISMO, DEA, refund cycle and repeat rates
steps: List the 8 steps: delivery promise and tracking, returns, unboxing, replenishment and nudges, quiz personalization, loyalty and VIP, gifts and community, win-back.
Attach the exit gate metric and its current value to each step.
Mark which step is in progress and which is blocked behind it.
Review the gates monthly and do not start a later step early without a written override.

test.method: Review gate status monthly and confirm no step is skipped ahead of an unmet gate.

title: Require every journey map to name at least one touchpoint it will change
hypothesis: If every journey mapping session must produce at least one changed touchpoint, then the exercise stays a management tool instead of becoming a one-time workshop deliverable that nothing acts on.

signal.check: A journey map was produced but no specific touchpoint change came out of it.

risk.note: A process rule for any journey mapping work.

prerequisites: A completed or planned journey map
steps: Require the mapping session to end with at least 1 named touchpoint change.
Assign an owner and a date to that change.
Keep the map as a living tool, updated as changes ship.
Reject a map with no attached change as incomplete.

test.method: Check 90 days later whether the named change actually shipped.

title: Make personalization change what the customer sees or gets, not just their first name
hypothesis: If personalization changes the actual product shown, fit, or replenishment timing instead of just inserting a first name, then it actually shortens the customer's time to satisfaction.

signal.check: Personalization in emails or on-site is limited to first-name tokens with no change to product, content or timing.

expected_effect.size: one cited on-site case reports a 23.28% uplift from an adaptive homepage carousel

risk.note: A personalization engine or logic build.

prerequisites: Customer behavior or quiz data to personalize against
steps: List current personalization limited to name tokens.
Identify 1 real change to make: quiz-driven fit, usage-timed replenishment, or on-site product ordering.
Build and test that change against a control group.
Retire name-token-only personalization claims from reporting.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for the real-personalization group against a control group after 60 days.

title: Earn personalization data through a value-adding quiz the customer knowingly answers
hypothesis: If personalization data is collected through a quiz the customer chooses to answer instead of opaque inference, then it avoids the 'creepy' reaction that causes immediate abandonment.

signal.check: Personalization or targeting relies on inferred or third-party data with no value-adding quiz offered to the customer.

risk.note: A quiz tool build or integration.

prerequisites: [web check: quiz tool options and pricing]
steps: Design a short quiz that helps the customer find the right product.
Make the value exchange clear: better recommendations in return for a few answers.
Avoid opaque inference or third-party data as the primary personalization source.
Feed quiz answers into product recommendations and post-purchase content.

test.method: Track quiz completion rate and quiz-buyer conversion versus non-quiz buyers after 60 days.

title: Keep the personalization quiz short and measure it against non-quiz buyers
hypothesis: If the quiz stays around 5 questions and its completion rate, buyer AOV and return rate get measured against non-quiz buyers, then quiz length gets tuned by evidence instead of guesswork.

signal.check: The quiz has many more than about 5 questions, or its impact on completion rate, AOV or return rate has never been measured against non-quiz buyers.

expected_effect.size: one case (Bare Anatomy) reports 35% lower CAC from a 75-plus-question quiz, a third-party write-up

risk.note: A quiz configuration and measurement change.

steps: Start near 5 questions unless category consideration clearly justifies more.
Never funnel every answer to the same product.
Track completion rate, quiz-buyer AOV and quiz-buyer return rate against non-quiz buyers.
Extend the quiz length only when a completion-rate test justifies it.

test.method: Compare completion rate and AOV before and after a quiz-length change.

title: Balance personalization against discovery, seasonality and ongoing testing
hypothesis: If recommendations are checked periodically for whether they narrow what shoppers see, then personalization does not quietly shrink the catalog a customer discovers.

signal.check: Product recommendations rely heavily on purchase history with no check on whether new or seasonal items ever surface.

risk.note: A recommendation-logic review.

steps: Review what share of shown recommendations are new versus history-based.
Add a discovery or seasonal slot into the recommendation logic.
Test whether the discovery slot changes overall conversion or AOV.
Re-check quarterly as the catalog changes.

test.method: Track the share of orders that include a discovery-slot item after 60 days.

title: Pair personalization with risk reversal or virtual try-on where the category supports it
hypothesis: If personalized recommendations are paired with a fit guarantee or virtual try-on in high-return categories like apparel, then the return rate drops instead of personalization alone trying to fix a fit problem.

signal.check: Personalized recommendations are live in a high-return category like apparel with no fit guarantee or virtual try-on paired with them.

expected_effect.size: mixed vendor sources report AR try-on cutting returns 25% to 45% in apparel with 30% to 50% base return rates

risk.note: May require a virtual try-on vendor or tool; verify pricing and fit before committing.

steps: Confirm the category has a high base return rate tied to fit.
Shortlist a virtual try-on or sizing tool if not already in place.
Pair personalized sizing recommendations with the try-on or fit guarantee.
Track return rate before and after.

test.method: Compare return rate for the paired approach against the prior personalization-only approach after 90 days.

does_not_apply_when: Categories with low fit-related return rates

title: Buy or use an existing app for search, ranking and merchandising instead of building it in-house
hypothesis: If search, ranking and merchandising run on a bought or partnered platform instead of custom-built infrastructure, then engineering effort stays on what actually differentiates the brand.

signal.check: The store has built or is planning to build its own search, ranking or merchandising engine in-house.

expected_effect.size: 1 vendor-side source, a Coveo GM's commercial position

risk.note: A platform decision with switching cost; verify vendor claims before committing.

prerequisites: [web check: search and merchandising vendor options, pricing]
steps: List what differentiates the brand: assortment, layout, supplier choices, persona.
List commodity capability: ranking, query understanding, catalog normalization.
Keep the differentiating list in-house.
Buy or partner for the commodity capability list.
Require the vendor to state its optimization objective and signals used.

test.method: Track engineering hours spent on search infrastructure before and after the switch.

title: Write the business objective and allowed signals before deploying any AI ranking or recommendation model
hypothesis: If the outcome metric and allowed signals are written down before an AI model goes live, then the model gets checked against a real goal instead of running as 'AI for AI's sake.'

signal.check: An AI ranking, search or recommendation model is live or planned with no written objective metric or list of allowed signals.

risk.note: A documentation step ahead of or during an AI deployment.

prerequisites: Candidate outcome metric: margin per visitor, conversion, or AOV
steps: Pick 1 outcome metric in advance: margin per visitor, conversion, or AOV.
List the signals the model is allowed to use.
Treat the model as probabilistic; monitor and correct it, do not treat it as ground truth.
Review the objective and signal list at each model update.

test.method: Track the chosen outcome metric before and after the model's next update.

title: Rank on-site search results by intent and business goal, not popularity alone
hypothesis: If search and category ranking combine typed intent with business goals, not just popularity, then a broad query surfaces the mix of products that actually serves the customer and the business.

signal.check: Search or category ranking sorts by popularity or best-sellers alone, with no adjustment for query intent or business goal.

expected_effect.size: one cited footwear client example lifted order value 'substantially' by ranking related categories together

risk.note: A search or merchandising configuration change.

prerequisites: Search or merchandising platform with ranking rule configuration
steps: Identify ambiguous queries where intent could mean more than one thing.
Combine typed query understanding with browsing context and history.
Add a business-goal weighting alongside popularity, for example surfacing adjacent categories.
Track order value and conversion for adjusted queries.

test.method: Compare AOV and conversion for adjusted-ranking queries against the popularity-only baseline after 30 days.

title: Remove repeated logins and long page-throughs from cart, checkout and account flows
hypothesis: If repeated logins and unnecessary multi-page throughs are removed from cart, checkout and account flows, then fewer interrupted shoppers abandon partway through.

signal.check: The cart, checkout or account flow requires logging in more than once, or has more page-throughs than necessary for a mobile shopper who may be interrupted.

risk.note: A UX and platform configuration change.

prerequisites: Access to checkout and account flow configuration
steps: Walk the cart, checkout and account flow as a customer on mobile.
Count every login prompt and page transition.
Remove any repeated login requirement.
Collapse unnecessary page-throughs, designing for a shopper who may be interrupted mid-flow.

test.method: Compare checkout completion rate before and after the flow simplification.

title: Free merchandisers from manual search and layout monitoring so they focus on assortment and supplier strategy
hypothesis: If tools handle dead search terms and layout policing automatically, then merchandisers spend their time on assortment, supplier and persona strategy instead of manual monitoring.

signal.check: Merchandisers currently spend significant time manually checking dead search terms and policing category layout.

risk.note: A tooling and workflow change.

prerequisites: Search and merchandising platform with automated monitoring features
steps: Audit how much merchandiser time goes to manual search and layout monitoring.
Turn on or configure automated alerts for dead search terms and layout issues.
Reallocate freed time to assortment, supplier and persona strategy work.
Track the time reallocation after 1 quarter.

test.method: Track merchandiser hours spent on strategy versus monitoring before and after.

title: Treat any markdown or clearance pricing as a costed decision against the discount-cohort penalty
hypothesis: If a markdown or clearance decision is checked against the discount-cohort penalty before it runs, then a slow week does not turn into a reflexive discount that quietly damages long-term LTGP.

signal.check: A markdown or clearance sale is planned mainly to defend a slow week's revenue, with no reference to the brand's own discount-cohort penalty.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a discipline gain preventing loss

risk.note: A decision-review step before the markdown runs.

steps: Pull the brand's own discount-cohort penalty from the audit.
Compare the expected front-end lift of the markdown against that penalty.
Approve the markdown only when the lift outweighs the known penalty.
Log the decision and its numbers for the next review.

test.method: Recompute the discount-cohort penalty for customers acquired during the markdown 90 days later.

title: Remove checkout friction: show total cost up front, offer guest checkout, cut fields, and remove dark patterns
hypothesis: If checkout shows total cost before the final step, offers guest checkout, cuts fields toward the necessary minimum, and removes dark patterns, then fewer shoppers abandon at the last step.

signal.check: Checkout hides shipping or tax until a late step, requires account creation, has more than about 7 to 8 fields, or contains a dark pattern like a pre-checked add-on or a hard-to-cancel flow.

expected_effect.size: one cited average cart abandonment rate is 70.22% across a 50-study meta-analysis

risk.note: A checkout configuration change; watch failed orders and support contacts after cutting fields, not just abandonment.

steps: Show total cost including shipping and tax before the final step.
Offer guest checkout as the default path.
Add express pay for returning buyers.
Cut form fields toward the 7 to 8 strictly necessary.
Remove dark patterns: hidden subscriptions, pre-checked add-ons, fake urgency, hard-to-cancel flows.
Watch failed orders and support contacts after cutting fields, not only the abandonment rate.

test.method: Track checkout-to-order conversion and failed-order rate for 30 days after the changes.

title: Confirm which orders are marketplace-fulfilled and exclude them from CXP workflows
hypothesis: If marketplace-fulfilled orders are flagged and excluded from branded tracking, unboxing and support workflows, then post-purchase effort does not get spent on orders the brand cannot actually touch after the sale.

signal.check: Branded tracking, unboxing or support workflows are being applied uniformly with no check for whether an order is marketplace-fulfilled and outside the brand's control.

risk.note: A data-tagging and workflow-exclusion step.

prerequisites: Order data tagged by fulfillment channel (brand-fulfilled vs marketplace-fulfilled)
steps: Tag every order as brand-fulfilled or marketplace-fulfilled.
Exclude marketplace-fulfilled orders from branded tracking, unboxing and support workflows built in this domain.
Report the share of orders that are marketplace-fulfilled and out of scope.
Verify the exclusion against brand data before relying on it.

test.method: Confirm the marketplace-fulfilled share matches actual marketplace order volume from the platform.

does_not_apply_when: Stores with no marketplace-fulfilled order volume

title: Track a customer retention rate for a fixed population, defined consistently at both ends of the window
hypothesis: If a fixed-population retention rate is computed with the same customer population and window defined at both the start and end, then the number stays comparable period to period instead of drifting from a shifting definition.

signal.check: Customer retention rate is reported with no clear definition of the starting and ending population, or the definition changes between reports.

risk.note: A definition and reporting fix.

prerequisites: Customer count data at 2 points in time, with new customers identifiable
steps: Define the population and the window once, in writing.
Compute CRR as (customers at end minus new customers in the period) divided by customers at start.
Use the same definition every period going forward.
Flag any period where the definition had to change.

test.method: Track CRR using the fixed definition for 2 consecutive periods and confirm it is comparable.

title: Produce a standard cohort readout with 3 written findings every reporting cycle
hypothesis: If a standard 1-page cohort readout with 3 named findings ships every cycle, then the weakest function, discount penalty and cohort trend are always visible to decision-makers instead of buried across separate reports.

signal.check: There is no standing cohort readout deliverable, or past readouts have not stated 3 clear findings.

risk.note: A recurring reporting build.

prerequisites: Cohort LTGP, repeat rate, F2 rate and top-20% share builds already in place
steps: Build the header: brand, data date, cohorts covered, windows.
Add the per-cohort table: customers acquired, Day-0 GP, LTGP series, repeat rates, F2 rate.
Add trailing-12-month top-20% share and the discount-code split with penalty.
Write 3 findings: the weakest function, the discount penalty if any, the cohort trend.
Note any caveats: cohorts too young, missing COGS, any unavailable figure.

test.method: Confirm the readout ships on schedule and the 3 findings change or get reaffirmed each cycle.

title: Run a full persona journey mapping session with Kano classification and a peak-end map
hypothesis: If 1 high-value persona's full journey gets mapped with Kano classification and a marked peak and end, then the fix list, the funded peak, and the touchpoint each change alters all come out of 1 session instead of scattered guesses.

signal.check: No structured journey mapping session with Kano classification and peak-end marking has been run for the highest-value persona.

risk.note: A workshop-style session; the output must ship at least 1 change to count (R128).

prerequisites: Cohort data to pick the highest-value persona
steps: Pick 1 persona: the highest-value cohort or the segment with the sharpest pain.
Decide the intended experience in 1 sentence and check current processes can deliver it.
Plot actions and emotional states across consideration, purchase, wait, delivery, use, support, return, repeat.
Classify each touchpoint by Kano: must-be, one-dimensional, attractive.
Tag each as a service or discretionary moment.
Mark the current peak, end, and any negative peak.
Draft the staff 'what if' checklist for service moments.
Output the fix list, the funded peak and end, and the touchpoint each change alters.

test.method: Confirm at least 1 named touchpoint change ships within 90 days of the session.

title: Write support reply templates for the 8 common contact types, checked for brand voice
hypothesis: If templates exist for WISMO, late delivery, damaged item, return request, refund status, cancellation, product question and complaint escalation, each checked blind for brand voice, then agents respond fast and consistently without sounding like a generic bot.

signal.check: Support agents write each reply from scratch, or existing templates have not been checked for brand voice.

risk.note: A writing and review exercise using the brand voice guide.

prerequisites: Brand voice guide, approved claims and policy limits
steps: Pull the brand voice guide and 3 examples of on-voice copy.
For each of the 8 contact types, write a template: the problem named, the fix with a date, what the customer needs to do, 1 human line.
State only policy the brand record confirms.
Mark variables in brackets, like order number and date.
Have someone who knows the brand read 3 templates blind and confirm the voice.
Version the set and review after every policy or tool change.

test.method: Track first-reply time and CSAT for templated contact types over 60 days.

title: Run a voice-of-customer process that starts with owned data and employee input before surveying customers
hypothesis: If ticket themes, refund reasons and review text get read first, then employees get asked, and a survey only runs for a question only customers can answer, then customers are not asked to check what the business should check itself.

signal.check: Customer surveys are the first or only tool used for voice of customer, with no review of owned data or employee input first.

risk.note: A sequencing and governance change on an existing or planned survey program.

prerequisites: Ticket, refund-reason, and review data access
steps: Do the owned-data homework first: ticket themes, refund reasons, review text, returns reasons, WISMO and DEA data.
Ask the support and fulfillment team what customers think, only once a plan to act exists.
Talk directly to 5 to 10 customers, including returners and lapsed buyers.
Run 1 short survey only for a remaining gap only customers can answer, with a named owner and budget to act.
Report survey scores only alongside cohort repeat rate and contribution, never alone.

test.method: Check whether the survey question set changed after the owned-data review, confirming it was not redundant.

title: Design every retention test with a named constraint, a pre-registered hypothesis, and a decision rule
hypothesis: If every retention test states the constraint, the metric, the minimum change worth acting on, the readout date, and the ship-iterate-stop rule before it launches, then the team decides on evidence instead of on how the data happens to look afterward.

signal.check: A retention test is planned or running with no written hypothesis, minimum meaningful change, readout date, or pre-registered decision rule.

risk.note: A test-planning template and discipline, not a live change by itself.

prerequisites: Named constraint from the cohort readout (F1, F2 or F3)
Chosen touchpoint from the journey map
steps: Name the constraint (F1, F2 or F3) and the touchpoint the test targets.
Pick the test class in order: structure and timing first, then offer, then messaging.
Write the hypothesis with the metric, current value, minimum change worth acting on, and window.
Choose randomized or matched-cohort splits.
Set the readout date at the metric's window plus 2 weeks for refunds.
Pre-register the decision rule: ship, iterate, or stop.
Log the test in a dated experiment file.

test.method: Confirm the decision matches the pre-registered rule once the readout date arrives.

title: Recompute every source's spoken example figure from raw numbers instead of reusing the rounded claim
hypothesis: If every worked example or spoken figure gets recomputed from its own stated inputs, then a presenter's rounding error never quietly becomes the brand's own number.

signal.check: A vendor or presenter's rounded spoken figure (like 'about 20 or 30 percent') is being repeated as a computed result without recomputing from the stated inputs.

risk.note: A verification step in reporting.

prerequisites: The raw inputs behind any cited worked example
steps: Find the stated inputs behind any cited example figure.
Recompute the result in code from those inputs.
Report the computed value, with the source's spoken value in brackets if it differs.
Never average repeat-rate or other benchmark figures from different sources with different populations or windows.

test.method: Spot-check 3 recently cited figures against their stated inputs.

title: Reserve second-purchase incentives for the first-to-second step only, never for loyal or subscriber customers
hypothesis: If a discount incentive is offered only at the first-to-second purchase step and never to loyal or subscriber customers, then the whole base does not get trained to wait for a deal that was only meant to test new-customer discovery.

signal.check: A discount code or incentive is being sent to loyal or subscriber customers as a matter of course, or the same incentive rule applies at every purchase stage.

risk.note: A flow and offer-rule change.

prerequisites: Customer journey-stage tagging: new, returning, loyal, subscriber
steps: Confirm which flows currently send an incentive.
Keep an incentive only at the first-to-second purchase step, as a stated test.
Remove incentives from loyal and subscriber tier messaging.
Measure the first-to-second incentive against f2_rate_90 and 365-day LTGP, and run any code through the discount-cohort audit.

test.method: Track discount reliance and repeat rate for the loyal tier 90 days after removing incentives.

title: Log AI-referred and agent traffic share every month to watch for a funnel shift
hypothesis: If AI-referred and shopping-agent traffic share is logged monthly, then a real shift toward AI-mediated shopping gets caught early instead of discovered only after it has already changed the funnel.

signal.check: Referrer data is not being tagged or reviewed for AI platform or shopping-agent traffic.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a monitoring build; one source's own heuristic trigger is 10% to 20% adoption

risk.note: An analytics tagging step.

steps: Tag known AI platform and agent referrers in analytics.
Report AI-referred and agent traffic share monthly.
Set a share threshold (the source's own heuristic is 10% to 20%) that triggers a funnel review.
Open a funnel review once that share is reached.

test.method: Track the monthly AI-referred traffic share trend for 2 quarters.

title: Run a quarterly unbranded prompt audit across major AI platforms to track brand visibility
hypothesis: If a set of unbranded prompts an ideal customer would ask gets run across the major AI answer platforms each quarter, then a real change in AI discoverability shows up in a trend instead of being judged from 1 noisy run.

signal.check: No unbranded prompt audit exists to track how or whether the brand gets mentioned in AI platform answers.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source calls single-run LLM ranking noisy and inconsistent

risk.note: A recurring manual or semi-automated audit.

prerequisites: List of unbranded prompts an ideal customer would ask
steps: Build a list of unbranded prompts an ideal customer might ask.
Run them across ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini on 3 separate days each quarter.
Record mentions and cited sources.
Treat any single run as noise; only trust the quarter-over-quarter trend.

test.method: Compare mention and citation counts quarter over quarter for 1 year.

title: Label every vendor or brand case number as a claim, not a benchmark, in every report
hypothesis: If every vendor or brand case figure in a report carries the word claim next to it, then the founder never mistakes 1 vendor's self-reported result for a benchmark the store should expect to hit.

signal.check: A report, deck or dashboard states a vendor or brand case figure (a percentage lift, an ROI multiple) with no indication that it is a claim rather than a measured or expected result.

expected_effect.size: unknown, an honesty and expectation-setting fix

risk.note: A writing and reporting-template rule.

prerequisites: A reporting or deck template used for founder updates
steps: Scan the last 3 reports or decks for vendor or brand case figures.
Add the word claim next to every one that is not the brand's own measured result.
Update the reporting template so this is the default going forward.
Reserve unlabeled numbers for the brand's own measured data only.

test.method: Audit the next 3 reports for any unlabeled vendor or case figure.

title: Time replenishment nudges to 75 percent of the product's usage cycle, capped at 2 messages per cycle
hypothesis: If a replenishment nudge fires at 75% of the product's real usage cycle and never more than twice per cycle, then the message lands when the customer is actually running low instead of on an arbitrary fixed day count.

signal.check: Replenishment nudges send on a fixed day count unrelated to the product's real usage cycle, or send more than twice within 1 cycle.

expected_effect.size: one source reports replenishment conversion of 8% to 15% versus 1% to 3% for general promos, a vendor benchmark

risk.note: A flow trigger and timing change.

prerequisites: Pack size and usage cadence per SKU, or observed median reorder interval
steps: Compute usage_cycle_days per SKU from pack size and daily usage, or use the observed median reorder interval.
Set the trigger at 75% of that usage cycle.
Cap replenishment messages at 2 per cycle.
Frame the message as usefulness, not a generic promo.
Track f2_rate_90 and repeat rate before and after the change.

test.method: Compare replenishment-triggered conversion rate against general promo conversion rate over 90 days.

does_not_apply_when: Durable, one-off products with no repeat usage cycle to time against
